MOTIONS
America’s Cup 2013—Emirates Team New Zealand

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I seek leave to move without
notice a motion in recognition of Team New Zealand’s efforts in the America’s Cup.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That this House congratul ate Emirates Team New
Zealand on its hard-fought campaign in the 2013 America’s Cup in San Francisco .
Although the result was not what we were hoping for, we send congratulations to Oracle
Team USA and admire their fighting spirit  and the ongoing improvements made to stay
in the match and eventually take the c up. To Emirates Team New Zealand, you have
made us proud, and we have loved every moment of watching your boat Aotearoa
literally fly around San Francisco Bay. You caught the interest and attention of so many
New Zealanders who did not expect to admire and become involved in the America’s
Cup contest. You have competed hard on the water, and have conducted yourselves
with dignity and professionalism off the wa ter. On behalf of 4.5 million Kiwis,
congratulations on a great campaign.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I rise on behalf of the New
Zealand Labour Party to s upport the motion. We congratulat e Oracle Team USA on a
successful defence of the America’s Cup. It was a truly remarkable comeback. We send
our commiserations to Grant Dalton, to Dean  Barker, and to the crew that made New
Zealanders so proud. The sporting hopes of the nation were with Emirates Team New
Zealand on every tack, every gybe, and every fo il. The crew did their very best, and it
was a fantastic effort. We c ongratulate them. We record our admiration for the Kiwi
ingenuity and innovation that saw New Z ealand boating and computer technology
displayed to the world as the best in the world. That expertise, together with New
Zealand’s extraordinary sailing excellence,  was just not quite enough on the day, and
we, again, commiserate with Emirates Team New Zealand for gettin g so close but not
quite winning.
Can I pass on our admiration for how dignifi ed they have been in defeat. We should
also be proud that in Oracle’s time of need they reached out to New Zealanders in order
to get the extra boat speed that  they needed. This is truly an event that has brought New
Zealanders together. As Grant Robertson said to me earlier, he understood that
somewhere in a bar in San Francisco it ha s even brought Steven  Joyce and Trevor
Mallard together singing Dave Dobbyn songs like “Loyal”.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: What a bugger, eh? What a race! We got
this close; they got this close. New Zealan ders all over the worl d have been cheering
Dean Barker, his team, and al l of the people who have work ed so hard to support this
race. My message is do not worry, because New Zealanders are still behind you, Dean
Barker, and all your team for all the amazing work you have done, no matter what the
result. The catamarans are so closely matche d that there was some tantalising racing,
with those flying catamarans travelling faster  than the speed of wind, and with lead
changes, yachts on the edge of tipping over—what I heard one wit describe as “the cock
of a dog’s leg”—and teams finishing within ju st seconds of each other. Race 10 of the
final will no doubt be one of the greatest ya cht races of all time, but it was also a
13770 Motions 26 Sep 2013
turning-point race. Well done to Oracle Team USA. It really, truly was some comeback.
To Team New Zealand—you did your country proud. Our hearts go out to you at this
time of great agony over the result, having come so close.
I suspect that technology was the winner  on the day for this cup—technology largely
built by New Zealanders. We can be doubly pr oud that both boats were built mostly by
New Zealanders here in New Zealand, and that Auckland is  now home to some of the
most advanced boatbuilding t echniques in the wo rld. This America’s Cup will be good
not only for our high-tech mari ne manufacturing industry but also for the thousands of
bright New Zealanders whom it employs. Team New Zealand, you have provided us
with a vision of a smart and green economy a nd a legacy that will not be lost, and there
is, of course, always next time.
Plus it is not all bad news on the sports  front today. Let us congratulate the New
Zealand Football Ferns, which won the Va lais Cup in Switzerland this morning—a
historic win for our women’s football t eam—and congratulations to New Zealand’s
Amber Hearn, who was named player of the tournament. Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: New Zealand First joins other parties in the
House in congratulating Team New Zealand. The final result of the America’s Cup,
even though a disappointment, when we came so close to winning, is  a time to reflect
on what New Zealanders are capable of  achieving. Team New Zealand performed
superbly against the scale and wealth of th e United States team, a team that had the
resources and the money to be able to bring in whomever and whatever it wanted at the
last minute, a team for whom money was no object. Olympic champions and advanced
technology were available to  the United States team—jus t a phone call away, at the
snap of the fingers, never mind the cost. And there is the irony that the winning boat
was actually built in New Zealand. In that sense, New Zealand is a winner.
Our boat builders have shown that they ha ve excellence in the world, just as our
sailors have shown through regattas the wo rld over, in every winning international
team, that they are also the best in the world. New Zealand First congratulates Team
New Zealand on their performance in the Am erica’s Cup in San Francisco. We applaud
Dean Barker, the crew, and all who contribu ted to this outstanding effort. We applaud
the families and the friends of the crew, and the legion of fine, patriotic supporters who
outlaid such time and effort, who stuc k by their team—our team—through thick and
thin, through the good times and the bad, right to the bitter end, a nd who are still there
for our boys.
We applaud Team New Zealand for their sportsmanship. We applaud them for their
grit and determination. We applaud their conduct as exemplary ambassadors for New
Zealand. In their gracious and commendabl e second placing—a silver medal for the
silver fern team—they have enhanced New Zealand’s reputation. The world sees us and
them in the light of old-fashioned good sportsmanship and gentlemanly conduct, and
that will serve us well going into the future and into the next 4 years, because, like
everyone else, I am sure that Team New Zealand will be back for another crack the next
time the auld mug is up for grabs.
Whatever happens next time, New Zeala nd and New Zealanders will be at the
forefront of the competition for yachting’s gr eatest prize—the prize that is rightfully
ours and will be again. New Zealanders will build the next generation of America’s Cup
boats, and New Zealanders will crew them . One day we will bring the cup home again.
This is not a time for mourning. It is not a time for disappoi ntment. It is a time for all
New Zealanders to say to our team “We ll done. Good on you. New Zealand is proud of
you.” Thank you.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker, kia
ora tātou katoa. Hei whaiwhai haere i te āhuatanga o te kōrero a ngā kaikōrero i mua i a
26 Sep 2013 Motions 13771
au, ko t āku he tautoko i ng ā kōrero katoa. Me mihi r ā ki a r ātou, ki a Dean Barker, me
tana kāhui, ki a Grant Dalton, r ātou katoa i angitu, i m āia ki te tū i te mura o te ahi, e ai
ki ngā kōrero. Ko te pai o t ērā hunga i te ata nei k āre i tuohu te m āhunga, kāre i piko te
tuarā, kāre i taka te ngutu o te waha, kāre i noho whakamuri ēngari i māia, i angitu, i aro
nui ki te kaupapa i wh āia e r ātou i te ata nei ka mutu, i ng ā wiki e 3 kua hipa ake. Me
mihi ki a r ātou ka tika m ō te āhuatanga o te t ū, he t ū tangata, he t ū tika, he t ū m ō te
motu e noho mai nei i te w ā kāinga, otirā, kāore e kore ko ng ā mea o Aotearoa wh ānui
tonu i te ao.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and greetings to us all. To follow on with the tenor of the
sentiments by speakers before me, I endorse all the tributes accord ed. We must indeed
express a tribute to them, Dean Barker, his crew, Grant Dalton, all of them who fought
on and according to accounts were tenacious at the battle-front. What was wonderful
about that group this morning was that the he ad did not cower, the back did not bend,
and the lip did not drop. They did not hold back but were relentless, courageous, and
remained focused on what they were trying to achieve this morning, and of course over
the past 3 weeks. We must pay them a tribut e indeed for the stance they took for
humanity, for the righteous, and for the ones of the nation that  remained here at home,
and without a doubt for the ones from New Zealand worldwide.]
I join the words of congratulations to our team. They did us proud, and as I said,
they did not step back, they did not drop th eir heads or their lips, they focused on the
task right through to the end, and we can be  proud of them. I think you can learn a lot
from studying some names. I had a quick Google of the word “oracle”, and apparently it
means a person or thing regarded as an infallible authority. But if we look at Team New
Zealand—and I suppose that is th e catch for all of us—every one of us finds a space in
Team New Zealand. Ka mihi ki a rātou ka tika.
[We must indeed pay a tribute to them.]
The great thing about our nation, I suppose, is the connections that we have. At home
we can be proud of people like Ben Malcolm and Warren Houston, whose art adorns the
hull of Aotearoa of Team New Zealand. Also, I thi nk we can admire the graphics of
Ngāti Kahungunu and Ng āpuhi designer Ian Taylor, who I think captured the world
with those graphics, but most im portant, I think, is the tie-in. P ēnei i a au a M āori nei,
ka kite atu i te hononga o te waka hourua me t ēnei waka—me k ī, e ai ki ng ā kōrero o
aku tūpuna i whakawhiti mai i Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa i te waka hourua. I ngā rā tata kua
hipa ake, ar ā, ko taua waka, ko taua āhua an ō r ā, he waka hourua, ā, me k ī koina te
kotahitanga o te whakaaro ao Māori, ao Pākehā. Ko ētahi ka kī, kāre he wāhanga o te ao
Māori ki roto i t ēnei o ng ā kaupapa. Ko t āku, ko te k ī atu, ē, kai roto i taku DNA t ērā
āhuatanga, mai i ōku tūpuna, i ōku mātua. Nō reira, koinei au e whai w āhi i roto i t ēnei
o ng ā kaupapa ahakoa, ko te waka-ama, ko te waka hourua r ānei, he waka tonu, ā,
koinei te āhuatanga o ōku tūpuna.
[Like me as a M āori, I can see the connection of the double-hulled canoe with this
vessel—that is to say, according to my an cestors they traversed the Pacific Ocean in a
double-hulled canoe. In days just past we ha ve that similar vessel type doing the same
thing. Let us suggest that it is the merging of M āori and non-M āori minds together as
one. Some might say that M āoridom has no part to play in this of the ventures. But I
would respond by saying steady on, that aspect  from my ancestors and parents is in my
DNA. It is for this reason, therefore, that I am able to participate in this of the ventures,
be it an outrigger vessel or a double-hulled one, it is st ill a canoe. As  far as my
ancestors are concerned, this situation is still there.]
I think we can be proud to fo cus not just on th e yacht race but on the presentation of
ourselves as a nation. I want to acknowledge the efforts of Ng āti Whātua Ōrākei and Te
Puni Kōkiri. I acknowledge the Minister of M āori Affairs, Pita Sharples, for putting us
13772 Motions 26 Sep 2013
on the map, alongside many others, I am sure, with the Waka M āori, which has
showcased the many tourism aspects and busin ess links to the USA and indeed to the
world. It is said that over  300,000 people a day went across th e Oakland Bridge just to
that location. So there will be benefits desp ite the sadness of the day, I am sure. Hei
whakakōpani i taku kōrero, me kī, kua kite nei tātou i tēnei tau kua hipa ake, e māia ana
a Aotearoa ki roto i t ēnei āhuatanga. Ko wai ka m ōhio m ēnā ka hoki atu an ō r ā ki te
pakanga i te pakanga pai. I te rā nei, ā, me tū tika tātou i te mea, ahakoa kāre i eke, ko te
ngākau ka taea te kī, ā, i eke ā-ngākau, i eke ā-wairua. Tēnā koutou, kia ora tātou katoa.
[To close my address, let us say we have witnessed just how resilient New Zealand
has been in the year just past in regards to this situation. Who is to know whether we
will ever go back again to engage in the good fight . In respect to this day, we must be
upright because even though we did not make it, we can still say within us that we made
it heart and spirit-wise. Congratulations to you collectively, and to us all.]

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: On behalf of the ACT Party and the people
of the Epsom electorate I want to congrat ulate Emirates Team New Zealand on their
competitive performance in the America’s Cup. I was privileged to be Minister of Sport,
Fitness and Leisure when the cup arrived from San Diego, and later I handed it over as
part of a delegation while I was Mayor of Auckland.
Team New Zealand did not get the result we  wanted, but they s hould be very proud
of the way they fought right to the end. Dean  Barker, Grant Dalton, and the rest of the
team worked hard to first win the Loui s Vuitton Cup and then push Oracle Team USA
right to the end, in a competition that many commentators thought would be all one-way
traffic. Their graciousness in defeat show s what great sportsmen and ambassadors New
Zealanders are. Ultimate congratulations  must also go to Oracle Team USA on its
stunning win of the 34th America’s Cup. Its win will be remembered as one of the great
sporting comebacks, and it contributed to one of the most exciting America’s Cup races
in history.
It is important today that we record and place on the record the huge contribution and
loyalty of the corporate sponsors. New Z ealand is a nation of sailors, and we can
appreciate a great competition, which the Am erica’s Cup has proved to be. We did not
win. However, the innovation and skills of Ne w Zealanders contributed significantly to
both teams, and that is something we can all be very proud of.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I rise on behalf of United Future
to associate myself with the sentiments that  others have expressed during this debate. I
happen to be one of those curmudgeonly yachting enthusiasts who did not think that the
advent of these giant catamarans was appropr iate for the America’s Cup tradition, and
who wondered whether the public would actuall y be seized by the event or would just
see it as big boys with big toys. The activ ities of Team New Z ealand over the last
several weeks, and particularly over the last  19 days, have proven to me how wrong my
fears were. This event has cap tured the public imagination. It was interesting, staring
out my window in a forlorn moment during the race this morning, to see virtually no
traffic in the streets of Wellington. People were actually glued to  television sets or
radios or streaming video, etc., because the nation had taken this event to its heart.
We wondered a lot over the last week, I guess, how it could be  that on Saturday
morning we were poised for victory but fo r some fickle wind and running out of time
when we were just a few seconds away fr om crossing the line, to the situation on
Thursday, when Team New Zealand, with everyone’s hopes on its back, was fighting
for grim survival. That is the magic of match racing of this particular calibre. Every tack
and turn, every twist,  every gybe, every foil, every sail  change, and every tacticians’
discussion that we have all been witness to over the last few days has, I think, brought
home the sheer rush of adrenalin that everyone gets watching this degree of sport.
26 Sep 2013 Motions 13773
It is true that this has been described in some quarters as being more a victory for
technology than for sport. Ce rtainly, technological advancement and the vast amount of
dollars invested by both teams to bring the latest degree of  technology and skill to their
operation was relevant, but at the end of the day you cannot take the event away from
the individual sailors who competed, both for Emirates Team New Zealand and for
Oracle Team USA. It was their skill, their determination, their raw strength, and their
courage that achieved the results that they did.
We can take solace in the performance of  our team, the dignity with which they
embraced their defeat, and the goodwill that they have created between New Zealand
and San Francisco. I notice that the Mayor of  San Francisco said today that two great
things about this cup were, one, that the United States won, and, two, that firm bonds
were formed with New Zealand by the city of San Francisco. Although we can take all
of those as positives, we must congratul ate Oracle Team USA on a simply stunning
performance. And we can note with some satis faction that of the crew members of that
boat there were, I think, some eight New Zealanders, the boat was built in New Zealand,
and there is a long New Zealand tradition, so if we want to stretch it, we can claim that
we all won today. I think there were two Americans on the boat, I say to my colleague.
What is important now, though, is that we do not wallow in self-pity and gloom
because of defeat in this contest. We ta ke from it the positives. We congratulate our
team—Grant Dalton, Dean Barker, and all of them—on a job well done, and we move
forward. If anyone says that the money that was invested by the Government to achieve
this result was not money well spent, I comple tely defy that criticism because this has
been a very positive outcome for New Zealand. The challenge now is to make sure that
we learn the lessons, that we  regroup, that we get a bette r team together—even better
next time—and that next time, when we are on match point, we nail the event.
Motion agreed to.

items.text: Order! Leave is sought for that pa rticular course of action. Is there

Hawke’s Bay Water Management—Groundwater Modelling
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister of Science and

items.speaker: Innovation
items.text: Did GNS Science undertake work modelling the groundwater in the
Ruataniwha Plains in 2012 and 2013; and was the contract completed fully?
Hon NIKKI KAYE (Minister for Food Safety)  on behalf of the Minister of

items.speaker: Science and Innovation
items.text: Yes, I have been advised that GNS Science undertook
groundwater modelling work in relation to the Ruataniwha Plains during the 2012-13
year. I am advised GNS Science was contra cted by the Hawke’s Bay Regional Council
for four separate pieces of work. Three contracts were completed and invoiced. One
piece of work was not completed.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Did the Minister know that GNS  Science scientists raised
serious concerns about the accuracy of the regional council’s groundwater model, the
fundamental information underpinning the work?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am advised that the Hawke’ s Bay Regional Council opted to
change its management strategy for the Ruatan iwha Plains. That is the reason that has
been given.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I invite the member to repeat his question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Did the Minister know that GNS  Science scientists raised
serious concerns about the accuracy of the regional council’s groundwater model, which
was the fundamental information underpinning the report?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Just to build on my previous answer, I have said the reason
why the contract was terminated, but fr om my perspective—and I am obviously
answering on behalf of the Minister—he did not know that.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Were the GNS Science scientists working on the project
pressured by the regional council into completing a report on the dam, despite their
objecting strenuously to the accuracy of the information they were supplied to work
with by the regional council?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: The first thing that I would say is that the contractual
arrangements—and I want to make this poi nt—between GNS Science and the Hawke’s
Bay Regional Council are not something that Ministers would ever be involved in the
detail of, but the member does make an alle gation in his particular question. I have no
knowledge of that allegation.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Did GNS Science scientists insi st on recording their concerns
about the inaccuracy of the council’s groundwater model in  their updated report, at
which point the contract was terminated by the council?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I will just repeat what I have said before, which is that GNS
Science has hundreds of contracts. The first time I became aware of this issue was
today, so what the member is saying in te rms of his question I cannot verify. But I
would say again that the contracts between GNS Science and the Hawke’s Bay
26 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13775
Regional Council are exactly contracts betw een them. There are hundreds of contracts
every year. I cannot verify what the member is saying.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Was it not the case that GNS Science wanted to insert a
disclaimer in its updated report, which was that it took no responsibility for the accuracy
of the work because the model that the council provided to it was not fit for purpose—
the model was not accurate?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Obviously, I am answering th is question on behalf of the
Minister, so if the member does want to provi de me with further information, then I am
happy to have a look at that. The second thing I would say is that I am not aware, again,
of the facts that the member raises and I think that he should put them in writing to me.
But, thirdly, the point I would make to the me mber is that he is raising issues regarding
the Hawke’s Bay Regional Council. I am act ing for the Minister  of Science and
Innovation. If he has issues re garding a local aut hority, then I think there are other
processes whereby he can raise those issues.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: With regard to GNS Science, for which the Minister is
responsible, is it the case that an earl y report in August 2012, provided by GNS Science
to the council, has been used by the Hawk e’s Bay Regional Council in its application
around the dam, rather than using the February 2013 amended report, which highlighted
the GNS Science scientists’ concerns that the report was not accurate?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Again, I want to raise a couple of  points. The first is that the
gist of the member’s ques tions is around the actions of  the Hawke’s Bay Regional
Council. Again, I do not have responsibility for that. In te rms of the allegations he
makes regarding the involvement of GNS Scien ce, I cannot verify th e facts that he is
saying, so I would ask him to put them in writing to me after question time.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister able to confir m that the contract between GNS
Science and the Hawke’s Bay Regional Counc il was terminated by the regional council
when GNS Science wanted to put its written concerns into a report indicating that the
results of the report would not  be accurate because the mo del provided by the regional
council was wrong?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: In one of my previous answers I gave you what I have received
in terms of advice as to why the Hawke’s Bay Regional Council said the contract was
terminated, and it is that the council opted to change its management strategy for the
Ruataniwha Plains, meaning that the contracted modelling work was no longer
considered relevant. I am also advised that this is not unusual for this type of work.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is it not the case that the change in management that the
regional council was referring to was that the report it was getting from GNS Science
was not the kind of report it wanted because  GNS Science was determined to put into
the report its concerns about the accuracy  of the groundwater modelling that the
regional council provided to it?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Again, I think that there are a number of questions that the
member is asking that relate to the Hawke’s Bay Regional Council, for which I am not
responsible. If the member has questions for the council, I suggest he contact the
council directly. If he has a concern about a local authority, he might direct a question to
the Minister of Local Government. But again, I repeat what I have said before. If there
are things that he wants to provide furthe r information to me on, I am happy to receive
that after question time. In terms of the alle gations that he makes, I cannot verify what
he is saying.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister aware that two of the three GNS Science
scientists who worked on the report for the regional council and ra ised concerns about
the accuracy of the science provided by the council no longer work at GNS Science?
13776 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2013

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I cannot verify, agai n, the facts that the member raises. But
what I would say to the member, again, is th at from previous experience in terms of
question time—and I cannot verify what he ha s said—there may be a range of reasons
why particular individuals do not work for an organisation. It may have nothing to do
with the various conspiracy theories the member is putting forward.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: As the Minister of Science and Innovation, is he concerned that
science is not being listened to in the Tuk ituki catchment process around this dam, the
Department of Conservation’s scientific s ubmission has been suppressed, the concerns
of the Ministry for Primary Industries were suppressed, and now GNS Science
scientists’ concerns were also suppressed?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I disagree with the assertions made in that member’s question.
Economy—Business Confidence and Employment
2. Hon KATE WILKINSON (National—Waimakariri)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: What recent reports has he receiv ed on the economy—and particularly
indicators of business confidence and employment intentions?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There have been reports for some
time of increased business confidence. There are now some reports that that higher level
of confidence is flowing through to positive hi ring intentions. According to a report by
recruitment company TMP/Hudson Global Re sources, hiring expectations among New
Zealand employers are at their highest level in 5 years. The survey indicates that around
33 percent of 1,000 employers surveyed intend to  increase the number of jobs in their
organisations in the next quarter. In th e South Island around half of all employers
surveyed intend to hire more people in the next quarter.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: What were the main factors behind the improvement in the
employment intentions of businesses in the last quarter?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There will always be particular factors for particular
businesses, because more jobs ar e created business by business. The Hudson Report
notes that there is gr eater confidence around hous ehold consumption and
manufacturing. It also noted that employe rs who have missed out on opportunities due
to limited resources—that is, due to not ha ving enough people on their payroll in lean
times—are now more confident because they want to build up their numbers so that
they can pursue future opportunities and growth plans. For instance, this is reflected in
51 percent of employers in the construction, property, and engineering sector looking to
hire more people in the next quarter.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: What other reports has the Minister seen indicating a building
momentum in the labour market?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There is a range of other indicators showing a positive
attitude to the employment market. Online recruitment company SEEK reported that
91,000 jobs were advertised in the last 4 m onths—about 8,000 more than in the first 4
months of 2013. The strongest growth in  job advertising came from design and
architecture, up 35 percent; banking a nd financial services, up 26 percent;
administration and office support, up 15 percent; and trades and services, up 23 percent.
These are indications of intentions. Of cour se, we will be looking for signs that these
intentions are followed through to more jobs on the payroll.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: What policies is the Government implementing to help New
Zealand businesses become more competitive and have the confidence to invest, grow,
and employ more staff?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There is not one single policy that makes a difference, and
that is why the Government has set out the Business Growth Agenda, which details 300
initiatives across infrastructure, employmen t, education, natural resource management,
26 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13777
and so on. Each of these initia tives is aimed to assist busi nesses to make the decision to
invest another dollar and employ another person, and become more internationally
competitive. We are also working on making su re that we can have a more flexible
housing market, because a housing market with fast-rising prices poses a threat both to
our financial stability and al so to the competitiveness of  businesses, which need the
lowest interest rates and lowest exchange rate that we can have for as long as possible.
Tattooing—Safety and Hygiene Standards
3. BARBARA STEWART (NZ First) to the Minister of Health: What concerns, if
any, does he have about the level of “heavy metal” in tattoo inks in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Under this Government at the end of
2011 the Environmental Protection Authority in troduced a new standard that sets the
controls for tattoo inks, includi ng labelling, safety data shee ts, advertising, storage, and
safe disposal. The Environmental Protectio n Authority also re cently developed a
voluntary guideline to manage the risks asso ciated with the chemical composition of
tattoo inks. I am concerned at the results of a recent Ministry of Health survey of heavy
metal in tattoo inks, which found that 9 of 18 grams did not comply with the
Environmental Protection Authority guidelines.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: Is he concerned about the number of young New Zealanders
whose back-alley tattoos by an unlicense d operator unnecessar ily expose them to
infections, scarring, or even cancer?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The member sounds a warning that people do need to
consider. Many people may not be aware th at tattoo inks may pose harm from the
chemicals from which they are made. Making the results of this survey available will
provide useful information for tattoo arti sts when deciding which tattoo inks to
purchase, and it does also provide information for those people who are deciding
whether or not to have a tattoo.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: Will the Minister put tattoo kits on the list of medical devices in
order to restrict sales to only those operators with licences?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The primary response from the regulation side at the moment
is the Environmental Protection Authority’s  standard. That standard has voluntary
guidance. It has essentially been in for the last 18 months. I think the member raises an
issue that is similar to the issue of solaria. If it is clear that the industry is not responding
sufficiently to the voluntary guidelines, then there will need to be another response from
the regulatory authorities.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: Would the Minister consider following Australia’s example and
introduce an age restriction or parental cons ent law in order to protect the health of
young New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: My understanding is that I th ink that Parliament had an
opportunity to vote on that in some legislation in the early  2000s, and voted against it.
More particularly, I think that on the issue that the member has raised, quite rightly,
about heavy metals in tattoo inks, the Environmental Protection Authority advises that it
is not aware of those being regulated at a na tional level anywhere else. I think that what
is important is the fact th at people who are consideri ng having a tattoo should learn
about the various metals that are used in the tattoo procedure.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: Does he intend to take any act ion to remedy this situation for
concerned parents; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Ministry has published the results of its surveys,
including the brands, on its website, and ha s made that information available to the
Tattoo Artists Association of New Zealand. The Ministry ha s asked the association to
advise its members to use only inks that comply with the Environmental Protection
13778 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2013
Authority guidelines. The Ministry of Health  has also sent the report to the district
health board public health units , in order to inform their work with local tattooists on
safety and hygiene. Again, those people w ho are considering a tattoo should make
themselves aware of all the information that  is available in resp ect of any personal
safety risks.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: Does the Minister agree that unsafe practices by unlicensed tattoo
artists, which put New Zeala nders at the risk of hepa titis C and other blood-borne
illnesses, should be prevented at all cost?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: We would be concerned about unsafe practices by those who
are licensed and not licensed. One of those practices that  we and the Environmental
Protection Authority would like  to prevent is the use of these tattoo inks with heavy
metals that do not meet the compliance requi rement. That is the reason why we have
made those results available and why public health units wi ll be able to use that
information to inform their work with local tattooists.
Hawke’s Bay Water Management—Minister’s Involvement and Meeting with
Officials
4. Hon RUTH DYSON (Labour—Port Hills)  to the Minister of Conservation :
How could he say on 17 September 2013 “I did not know that this draft document even
existed until this morning” when his Weekly Report from 29 July 2013 stated a
submission should be lodged “requesting that  the Board requests further information by
way of an independent peer review of th e proposed approach to nutrient management
and the potential effect of the proposed nutri ent limits and targets on the freshwater
values in the Tukituki catchment”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member half quotes the
weekly report. What it actually said was: “The Department is evaluating the proposed
plan change and resource consents. The De partment’s preliminary view is that a
submission should be lodged to  the plan change ...”. That  does not say that a draft
submission had been prepared. I stand by my  statement that I did not know until 17
September that the 34-page submission that was leaked existed.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Why did he say to reporters on Thursday, 19 September: “There
was no mention to me of a draft submission. I did not know of the existence of a draft
submission.”, when the agenda for his m eeting with officials on Monday, 29 July
outlined the submission’s contents, he was br iefed on it, he expressed concern about it,
and he asked for a copy of it to be delivered to his office the next day?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The submission that was delive red to me the next day was
radically different from th e 34-page document that was leaked. I can only quote Doris
Johnston, who, I note, members opposite said to ld the truth when she said: “He never

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. In respect of the answer from
the Minister, I do not believe it addressed th e question that the Hon Ruth Dyson asked.
Her question was very specific. He began to talk about other aspects of submissions, but
not what she asked—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! On this occasion I do not  agree with the member. The
question asked—[ Interruption] Order! I will be asking th e Hon Clayton Cosgrove to
leave the Chamber if I get an interjection like that again. The question asked about what
the Minister said to report ers on a particular day, and I think the answer given by the
Hon Dr Nick Smith adequately addressed the question.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: What advice has the Minister recei ved on when the senior managers
in the Department of Conservation saw the leaked 34-page draft submission?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I am advised that Doris Johnston, who was on leave prior to
my meeting on 29 July, had not read the leak ed 34-page draft submission at the time of
26 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13779
my meeting. I can also quote from an email the next day from other senior managers,
which I am happy to table, which said this: “None of us have seen the submission or

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Did he, or any of his staff, ha ve any discussions  with officials

meeting with officials on Monday, 29 July, when the nitrate issue was going to be a key

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Did he have any part in the d ecision to establish the Government
fund for irrigation infrastructure from wh ich $1.67 million has been granted for the
Ruataniwha Dam project?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: For 3 years I was the Minister for the Environment. I had
an intense interest in water issues. Include d in that was achieving the National Policy
Statement for Freshwater Management. I ha d no direct involveme nt in the issues
relating to the investments around irrigation. That was led by the then Minister for
Primary Industries, who is currently the Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Does he agree with the comment in the briefing note to him from
Wednesday, 31 July, which noted: “… the department is not submitting on the one-
nutrient management approach as the conser vation values of the Tukituki catchment do
not justify the resource investment required.”,  in light of the fact that the submission on
that very point had already been written?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: In the substantive briefing th at I received on 31 July, there
were two substantive reasons given for not  proceeding with a submission on the plan
change issues around nutrients. The first of those was that the Department of
Conservation accepted that the National Inst itute of Water and Atmospheric Research
(NIWA) science was robust, a nd the NIWA science was different from what some staff
at the Department of Conservation had. The second was that the amount of resource, the
amount of money that would need to be spent, to contest the NIWA position—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: They’d already done it.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, because they would require witnesses, and the evidence
would be larger than what could be justified.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: When does the Minister believe th e department changed its position
and why?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The key Department of C onservation staff member who
wrote the weekly report with the prelim inary view, saying that we should lodge a
submission on nutrient issues, wrote that on Thursday, 25 July. On Friday, 26 July he
attended a full day’s meeting convened by th e Hawke’s Bay Regional Council, with all
the scientists and advisers from NIWA and the like. At the end of that meeting on the
Friday, he told the regional council that th e Department of Conservation’s submission
was likely to focus on only the inundation i ssue and not the plan change issue over

Tuesday, 30 July an email stated that he and the other planning managers “are not
convinced we should be submitting on the plan change”, and that was confirmed as the

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Does he agree with the comment in the briefing note to him of
Wednesday, 31 July, which noted: “… the Department is not submitting on the one-
nutrient management approach as the conser vation values of the Tukituki catchment do
not justify the resource investment require d.”, given that the T ukituki catchment and
estuary is a significant conservation area in th e regional coastal plan, is noted as one of

the areas with important natural and historic values in the Hawke’s Bay conservancy
coastal environment, is a recommended area for protection under the department’s

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH

the report. What that report actually said in the summary was that the Tukituki value

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: I seek leave to table two document s. Can I say, first of all, that

Documents, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I seek leave of the House to table an email between senior
Department of Conservation managers on 30 Ju ly that makes it plain that the senior
managers were not convinced of the merits to submit on the plan ch ange and that none

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The document has been we ll explained. Leave is sought to

will be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Could I just ask for your

Welfare Reforms—Long-term Welfare Dependence and Initiatives Targeting
Young People
5. Hon PHIL HEATLEY (National—Whangarei)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What recent announcements has she ma de about the cost of long-term
welfare dependency?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Today the latest
annual valuation of the welfare system ha s been released. The June 2012 valuation
shows that the current lifetim e liability is $86.8 billion. L eaving aside the effect of
interest rates adding $13.4 billion, we have actively reduced the liability by $3 billion
due to fewer people being on benefit, par ticularly the unemployment benefit and the
domestic purposes benefit. This is a strong indication that changes that this Government
has made to the welfare system are working well and that efforts to reduce long-term
welfare dependency are making a difference.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Heatley
items.text: What does the valuation tell us about young people?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We now know that youth spend an average of 18.9 years
on benefit if they go on as teenagers,  costing $239,000 over a lifetime. The average
young beneficiary has a 43 percent chance of be ing on benefit in 15 years’ time, and 25
percent of youth are expected to be on a be nefit 40 years after the valuation date. Sixty
percent of those beneficiaries currently aged  30 to 39 came on to be nefit as a teenager.
This clearly shows that this Government’s focus last year on youth in the new Youth
Service was exactly where our focus needed to be.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Heatley
items.text: What is the Government doing to actively target young people
most likely to be on welfare long-term?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: As I have stated, we have focused welfare reforms on
young people. It is where our focus needs to be. In Budget 2011 an extra $287 million
was targeted at young people on benefits. This included child assistance for teen
parents, and it included the card. It was a bout money management, it was about getting
them into budgeting services, it was about maki ng sure that they are in education, and it
is making a difference. Budget 2012 included another $188 million for reforms that
provide more support. The investment appr oach has changed the entire focus of the
welfare system, and it is ensuring that we are putting support where it is needed most.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Is sending people without jobs off to Australia to get jobs the best
strategy she can manage to reduce long-term welfare dependency?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: That would be a no. There is actually a lot of work here,
and there is a lot of—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: That’s where they’re going.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Well, actually, most of them are not. The numbers that
are going to Australia have re duced. The member might want to look up the facts to be
assured of that. We are seeing more than 1,500 a week going off to go into jobs. That is
just those who are going into jobs. Anothe r 2,000 are going off to go into different
directions and because  relationships have changed, but , actually, 1,500 are going into
jobs, which I think is pretty extraordinary.
Housing, Affordable—First-home Buyers, Mortgages, and Auckland Property
Market
6. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister of Finance:
What is the range of estimate s, if any, of the number of first home buyers in Auckland
13782 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2013
who will be excluded from the housing market due to the new Loan to Value ratio
restrictions?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No estimates have been provided on
people excluded from Auckland or any other market. We need to keep in mind here that
the measures taken by the Reserve Bank have been described by the bank as temporary
measures in order to preserve stability in the financial system. What I can say to the
member, though, is that in consultation with the Government the Reserve Bank advised
that, on average, 30 percent of new lending by value is high loan-to-value ratio, and it
was estimated that around 40 percent of high loan-to-value ratio lending is to first-home
buyers. The bank also advised that of the 20,000 to 30,000 first-home buyers each year
nationwide—and it is, appare ntly, difficult to identify all first-home buyers—13,000 to
19,000 would obtain a high loan-to-value ratio loan and, of those, up to 12,000 will get
a loan. The remaining 6,000 to 8,000 will make the choice of either looking at a cheaper
property or delaying their purchase while th ey save a higher deposit. As the Reserve
Bank noted at the time, these numbers are di fficult to estimate, and, as important, they
do not take account of the Government’s policy changes in support of first-home
buyers.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given that answer, is he joini ng Sam Lotu-Iiga in asserting that
there are more cheap houses available to buy in Auckland that these first-home buyers
just are not clever enough to find?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am simply outlining for hi m the choices that first-home
buyers will be making.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: There are no affordable homes in Auckland.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, if there are no affordab le houses in Auckland, it is
because under Labour none got built, whereas under this Government they are starting
to get built. That is really good news. The fact is that first-home buyers—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Five long years.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, we welcome Labour’s support for our announcements
of more houses on the ground sooner over the next few months.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How many affordable homes have  been built in Auckland over
the last 5 years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Until we got agreement with Auckland Council that its
planning rules were preventing the building of  affordable homes, the answer is not
many. Now that we have agreement from Auck land Council to change its plan to allow
more affordable homes, we will be able to get on with building them. Secondly, the
Government has been working through the Housing New Zealand Corporation to get
into the provision of medium-density affordab le homes, and I have to say that that has
proven—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: They voted against it.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Against? Those members voted against that, but we are
continuing anyway.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Has he been advised by the Prime Minister why the Prime
Minister claimed in June that there would be an exemption from loan-to-value ratio
restrictions for first-home buyers?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Prime Minister did not claim that. What he said was that
he gave his view to the Reserve Bank as part of the consultation. On this side of the
House, though, old-fashioned as it may s ound, we respect the independence of the
Reserve Bank because we know what a mess this economy got into when politicians
were setting interest rates and running m onetary policy, and now the Opposition wants
to also run the housing market. The Reserve Bank’s independence is there in order to
avoid a repetition of the dangerous situati on of 2008, with which that Labour Party is
26 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13783
familiar, and in order to secure financial stability and lower interest rates. The Prime
Minister gave his view. The Governor of the Reserve Bank made his decision.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What steps is the Government taking to support first-home buyers
and improve access to affordable housing?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: First of all, I say to that member and to the Parliament that
the housing market in New Zealand faces two significant risks. One is that it becomes a
source of the kind of financ ial instability we saw as recently as 2008, when this
Parliament supported the Government wr iting a sovereign guarantee for over $100
billion of banking assets to make sure our economy did not go down the toilet.
Whatever cheap politics there might be in part of the housing market, that is a
fundamental responsibility of  the Parliament and the Reserve Bank, and we are
honouring that responsibility. Within the scope  of that job, the Government has moved
to pass legislation to ensu re that we can get more houses on the ground sooner. We
passed that legislation, against the opposition of the Labour Party, just as it opposed the
Auckland Housing Accord.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The answer has gone on quite long enough.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he agree that the harshness of the Reserve Bank’s loan-to-
value ratio restrictions is due to National’ s 5 years of failure on housing and tax policy;
if not, why is the OECD concerned both about  New Zealand house prices, especially in
Auckland, and the tax biases that favour speculators over first-home buyers?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No; and the OECD has not made that point either. In fact—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Yes, they have.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: —it has not. If we think of the last 5 years, house prices
actually dropped by about 10 percent for a coup le of those years. During those years,
the Government started the process of creati ng the policy to ensure that we have more
houses on the ground. Labour has opposed—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! Again, that is a satisfactory answer.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What reports has he seen on alternative policies for first-home
buyers?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have seen a report just this morning that says: “… his
utterances could be damaging to long-term confidence in the economy … It is hard to
believe he would carry out the promise to over-ride the Reserve Bank’s independence to
exempt first-home seekers, if only because of  the obvious risk to their equity.”—that is,
getting first home buyers into houses that tu rn out to be worth less than what they
paid—“… it would be easy to weaken the bank’s legislated juri sdiction and do untold
damage to our economy. Mr Cunliffe’s stance is a worry.” That is today’s New Zealand
Herald editorial.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the reason the Minister of Fi nance refuses to reform what is
amongst the most favourable and distortionary tax laws for rental property investment
in the world and refuses to take practic al steps to improve housing affordability by
building affordable homes that his party fa vours property speculato rs over first-home
buyers, or is it just incompetence?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, the member is wrong about that. We made changes to
the taxation of property investment in the 2010 tax package, whic h is collecting over
half a billion dollars of extra tax. It is much more effective than a capital gains tax,
which the member said would come into practice over 15 years. It is also very clear that
a capital gains tax that does not cover all property is ineffective. They have got one in
Australia and it has made no difference whatsoever.
13784 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2013
Schools, Buildings—Funding and Property Management
7. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Associate Minister of

items.speaker: Education
items.text: What announcements has she made regarding school property?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: This week I was pleased to
announce a plan to transform the way that sc hool property is delivered in New Zealand.
Budget 2013 sets aside $134 million to support new schools and roll growth over the
next 4 years. I announced that $70 million ha s been allocated to establish three new
schools and 65 classrooms over the next 2 years. There will also be a programme
focusing on specific schools that require major develo pments. The Ministry of
Education is creating a fund of $300 m illion over 6 years to assist another
approximately 30 schools to deliver essential infrastructure and modernise their
facilities. These changes are about shifting from a one-size-fits-all approach to a system
that provides greater choice and flexibility for schools and students. I have had amazing
feedback across New Zealand. I am very proud to have made these announcements.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What specific measures does the new plan include?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: In addition to schools in Auckland, Hamilton, and Queenstown
the plan focuses on eight areas, including inve sting in areas of gr owth, helping schools
resolve outstanding property issues faster, providing grea ter support for major property
works, and offering a more flexible range of property services to schools. The Ministry
of Education is also establis hing an education infrastructure  service by the end of 2013
to offer schools a flexible ra nge of property management serv ices. There will also be a
dedicated team to resolve longstanding comp lex property issues, a nd an advisory board
to provide greater innovation, commercial expertise, and independent advice to the
Secretary for Education and Ministers. This Government is committed to investing in
education and making sure that our schools have  high-quality infrastr ucture in order to
achieve the best outcome for New Zealand students.
Bay of Plenty District Health Board—Diagnostic Testing and Whakatāne Hospital
Redevelopment
8. BRENDAN HORAN (Independent) to the Minister of Health: How long does it
take for microbiology samples to be taken fr om a patient in the Eastern Bay of Plenty
until the sample is cultured in the Pathla b microbiology laboratory in Tauranga, and is
he confident that the handling of samples and the time taken meets international medical
standards?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: That depends on where in the Eastern
Bay of Plenty the patient is and the nature of the sample taken from them. In response to
the member’s second question, yes, I am a ssured that the standard s, both national and
international, are being met.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Is the Minister aware that many Bay of Plenty medical
practitioners are concerned that they are ta king samples from patients as early as 8.30
a.m. that in Whakat āne are not collected from their practice until late in the afternoon
and then have to be transported to Taur anga, which is well be yond the best-practice
time of 2 hours, as stated in international medical standards?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: What I am advised is that every general practice in
Whakatāne does have material available to them that allows them to put these
specimens in a protective medium, which a llows the medium to work to keep the
microbiological sample testable within a period much longer than that—probably
between 24 and 48 hours. So what the memb er will recognise is that there is a
difference between the unprotected and pr otected microbiology specimens, and the
storage and transport times vary between these. Unprotected specimens should be
received by the laboratory within 2 hours. The only unprotected specimens produced in
the Eastern Bay of Plenty are those generated within the hospital, and these are
26 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13785
processed within that time frame. The ge neral practitioner - ge nerated microbiology
specimens must be protected, and all genera l practitioners are pr ovided with transport
media and have specific instructions and re quirements for their use. I am advised that
the time lines for transport meet national and international standards.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Is the Minister aware that in many secondary schools where nurses
are authorised to provide sexual health services, micr obiology samples, including
genital swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, are not uplifted until the end of the day,
when the best practice requires the samples to be inoculated on to a culture medium

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL

standards.

items.text: What other progress is being made  in relation to providing better

items.text: I am delighted to tell the H ouse that real progress is being

Homelessness—Definition, Statistics, and Access to Housing
9. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour) to the Minister of Housing: How many children
and young people are currently homeless, as defined by Statistics New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There is no agreed definition of
homelessness, and, by definition, it is actually  difficult to capture this data because the
census is collected via people’ s addresses. A recent analys is, though, by the University
of Otago of the 2006 census data identi fies 8,500 people under 15 with severely
inadequate housing, the majority of which is overcrowded. I note that in the period 2001
to 2006 the number in this group grew signifi cantly. In contrast, this Government is
investing $320 million on Project 324&5, which will reduce overcrowding, which is the
biggest group across these numbers.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: If he is on top of this issue and things really are getting better, why
has the Downtown Community Ministry ha d client numbers double each year since
2008, as has Lifewise in Auckland, whic h is increasingly s eeing young people and
children without housing?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I do not have specific inform ation on the data from those
specific organisations, but I would note that  the number of people on the Housing New
Zealand waiting lists was 4,300 in November, an d at the moment it is not too different
from that. That suggests that this is so mething of another manufactured crisis by
members opposite.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: On what—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The level of noise is ma king it hard for me to hear the
supplementary question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: On what grounds does he believe Housing New Zealand waiting
lists are a good measure of homelessness when he cut the list, changed the criteria, and
does not even consider a boarding house to be homelessness for the purposes of
Housing New Zealand?
26 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13787

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Can I firstly address the issue of the definition of
homelessness. In the survey the member quotes, it is referred to as “severely inadequate
housing”. Sixty-five percent of those who are in that definition are in situations where
there are too many adults and too many ch ildren in a household, and I note that that
number grew very significantly under the pr evious Government. The second issue is
whether I would consider people who are staying, for instance,  in cabins or in
emergency accommodation as being homeless. I would give them the definition of
being in emergency housing.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Has the Minister for Social Deve lopment raised any concerns with
him about young people’s access to housing, given that 90 percent of young people
Lifewise is working with ar e children who are leaving Ch ild, Youth and Family care at
17 with nowhere to go?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: My colleague Paula Bennett and I have had extensive
discussions, firstly, about the specific housi ng issues in west Auckland, and, secondly,
about the concerns she has around younger people and gettin g them into better quality
housing. I simply say to members opposite: wa tch this space in terms of the huge
investment of $2.7 billon—

items.speaker: Hon Tony Ryall
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: —$2.7 billion—the biggest inve stment ever in social
housing, which is taking place under this Government and was announced in this year’s
Budget.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Why, more than 3 years after the first of the Christchurch
earthquakes and after his own officials estimated that there are 7,400 homeless people in
the city, has he stood by while organi sations like the Young Women’s Christian
Association of Aotearoa have full waiting lists and are turning women and children
away, and when the Christchur ch City Mission has said it  is extremely worried about
the safety of children and that there is not enough happening?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I do not accept that there are 7,400 people in Christchurch
without a roof over their heads. That is not tr ue. It is true that there is a very large
housing challenge in Christchurch. That is why we have settled with the insurance
company and we are building a new house ever y single day in Christchurch. That is
why we have built four temporary accommoda tion villages. That is why we have
established the Canterbury Earthquake Te mporary Accommodation Service. I could
speak for over half an hour on what we are doing on housing in Christchurch.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I can assure the member that that  will not be occurring in question
time.

Young Offenders—Military-style Activity Camps and Alternative Policies
11. SUE MORONEY (Labour)  to the Associate Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: Does he support the continuation of boot camps for youth offenders?
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister for Social Development)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Associate Minister for Social Development
items.text: This Government does not operate boot
camps for young offenders. But if the member is referring to the military-style activity

items.text: Why has the Minister said that the boot camps model, as the Prime

items.text: I think we need to have this  in the context that these are

items.text: Is he disappointed, then, that Minister Bennett replaced Labour’s

offenders. So these are not those who are—

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Two conflicting reports have been brought to the
Minister’s attention. The first is a press release issued yesterday, stating that Te

that no young people had reoffende d. The second is a statement in Hansard dated 10
February 2010 that says that four of the eight Te Hurihanga graduates had reoffended.
26 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13789
What is so confusing about these two re ports is they were both by the Opposition
member Sue Moroney.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: What is the cost to the youth justice system and to the victims of the
325 crimes that were committed by graduates of the boot camp model in the first year of

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The cost would have been far higher if they had not gone
through a Military Activity Camp, because what we saw for those who did not was
reoffending that was more severe and mo re recidivist. Offending has gone down, and
the severity has as well.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that th e four re-offences she referred to

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I do not have that information in front of me, but what we

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Why does the Government not save a lot of pain, misery, and cost,

not the same young people—they are not th e same young people. Of the 23 who went

people are. You are simply not comparing the same young people.
Consumer Credit—Legislative Reform
12. Dr JIAN YANG (National) to the Minister of Consumer Affairs: How will the
Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Re form Bill target loan sharks and protect
New Zealand consumers?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The Credit Contracts and
Financial Services Law Reform Bill is the biggest overhaul of consumer credit law in a
decade, and will make wide-ranging changes to consumer credit and repossession law.
The changes represent a crack-down on unscr upulous lenders who prey on desperate
people and leave them and their families trap ped in a spiral of debt. These changes will
usher in an era where lenders must act re sponsibly, where consumers must have the
information they need, and where there ar e significant consequences for those who
breach the law. Rewriting the rules for consum er lending forms an important part of the
Business Growth Agenda of this Government to help boost trust and confidence in our
financial markets.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What changes are proposed in this  bill to ensure more informed
borrowers and more responsible lenders?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill
introduces a wide range of changes to ensure  more informed borrowers and responsible
lenders. Lenders will have to take responsibility for the likely effect of the credit
decisions they make for their customers.  There will be better controls against
misleading, deceptive, or confusing advertising of credit. I welcome cross-party support
for this bill, and I encourag e individuals and organisations  to make submissions as it
goes through its select committee process.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont

items.text: What analysis has he underta ken of the damage caused to

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.role: Minister fo r State Owned Enterprises
items.text: I move, That
Mighty River Power Limited be a public orga nisation for the purposes of the Standing

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: In case anybody missed that wonderful
speech by the Minister for State Owned Enterprises, that was the worst-performing
Minister in the history of Stat e-owned enterprises in this c ountry. It is interesting that
we are actually debating this motion—a moti on that follows a litany of stuff-ups and a
litany of incompetence by that particular Minister in all aspects of State-owned
enterprises. Primarily, this motion should ha ve been before the House when the mixed-
ownership model legislation wa s put in place in June last  year, but that Minister’s
incompetence in this portfolio is staggering—absolutely staggering.
We agree with this motion. We agree with it because it will a llow, finally, some
accountability of mixed-ownership model companie s; those that have been half sold off
to the private sector, like Mighty River Power, and those that are likely to be sold off in
part, like Meridian Energy. But if you look at the litany and the sham bles, this is the
peak of it for that Minister. On the matter of State-owned enterprises John Key in June
2011 said that the mixed-ownership model would yield, after the sales, $7 billion to $10
billion—that is how much he said would be raised from the sale of these assets. He then
claimed it would be $5 billion to $7 billion, and he now claims, after the 25c, I think, or
10 percent drop in the Migh ty River Power shares a nd the over billion-dollar
devaluation in Meridian Energy, that we are going to be—I think this is the quote from
the Prime Minister—“at the bottom end of the $5 billion range”.
The question for John Key and the question fo r this Government, of course, to quote
John Key, is that he now needs to show this House and show the people of New
Zealand the money, the cash. Look at the prom ises that were made in respect of the
Future Investment Fund from the sale of  State-owned enterprises—do you remember
that? The Future Investment Fund wa s going to fund hospitals and schools—
[Interruption]—kindergartens, and other things; kittens or whatever.
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13791
Then we find out two things. We find out that the money that is supposedly going to
be raised from the sale of these assets has been spent 10 or 15 times over, but worse
than that—worse than that—the money is se t aside not for hospitals and schools but so
that there is, say, $40 million to pay for the free shares of Mighty River Power and $100
million to bail out Solid Energy. Then if we have a look at some of the other allocations,
you would have to say it is simply bus iness-as-usual expe nditure—not hospitals,
bridges, roads, and schools. We have the immigrant management systems, closed
captioning on Parliament TV, and a replacem ent ground station for search and rescue
satellite systems. It is a whole lot of  business-as-usual expenditure—appropriate
expenditure but business-as-usual expend iture—that should be coming out of budgeted
expenditure not the revenue generated from the sale of these assets.
Then you have got to look at the combination of factors that have led to where we are
today. If you look at Meridian Energy, Meridi an Energy, of course, is balanced against
the huge risk of Rio Tinto going south before 1 January 2017. So what is the
Government’s plan with that? The Government  wanted to get that fiasco off the books
as quickly as possible. The Minister has b een asked time and time again why it was that
he and the Minister of Finance threw in $30 million worth of public money to a
company making billions of dollars on a multinational basis every year. He cited
repeatedly that this was to secure the jobs of those Southland workers; this would create
security. He even accused this side of the House of being an ti-jobs or being anti those
Southland jobs. Then we got him on radi o, and we asked whether he had got a
guarantee for the $30 million pieces of silver gi ven to Rio Tinto that those jobs would
be secure. The answer was no—that was on Ka thryn Ryan’s show. Then he was asked
whether he had even bothered—even bothered— to ask for a guarantee to secure those
jobs. The answer—no.
That gave the lie—the absolute lie—to the claim that $30 million of taxpayers’
money, a halving of the notice period, and ye t cheaper electricity for Rio Tinto was all
about securing those Southland jobs, because the Tuesday before the ink was dry on the
cheque, we know from the Southland Times that Rio Tinto had signalled the redundancy
of maintenance workers and a restructuring. And the Minister of Finance, aided and
abetted by the Minister for State Owned Enterpri ses, did not even have the brains or the
gumption to ask Rio Tinto—even if they were not going to get it; at least to roll the dice
and ask—whether it would guarantee those jobs  of those Southlanders up to 1 January
2017. Now they say that the reason they did not  have the brains or the gumption to ask
was because they do not interfere. Well, they  interfered in the pr ivate sector to the
extent that they picked a winner and used $30 million of taxpayers’ money to pick that
winner—and to halve the notice period, which signals to anybody buying Meridian
shares that if they pull the plug, we know what will happen to demand and supply and
the value of that company.
So we welcome this motion in respect of Mighty River Power. We welcome it
because it will actually allo w a select committee process around a financial review. It
will not, of course, allow us to gain info rmation through the Official Information Act
and it will limit what answers can be given in  this House by the Minister of Finance—
the shareholding Minister—and the Minister of State Owned Enterprises, because of the
so-called mixed-ownership model. What we ha ve got after all this—after all this—is a
litany of broken promises and a shambles in  terms of management of assets like Solid
Energy.
I mean, you have got to hand it to Tony Ry all. This guy has made history in this
Parliament. This is the worst-performing Mi nister for State Owned Enterprises in the
history of this Parliament, since State-ow ned enterprises were enacted in the 1980s.
Only that member and Bill English could st ep aside and stand there and watch as the
13792 Standing Orders 26 Sep 2013
coal price moved south. You just had to pick up the paper like the local village idiot to
work that one out. After literally 2 years of advice from Treasury and from their own
scoping consultants, UBS—which was charge d, ironically, with sc oping the company
for sale—after a litany of $23 million worth of bonuses that did not go to the blokes and
the women in the pit but went instead to th e guys in the flash suits in the palace in
Christchurch; after exorbitant expenditure; after Bill English, with the platinum-plated
spade, goes down to the lignite  plant in Southla nd, tosses the first sod—tosses the first
sod—and sings its praises, only to have it cl ose it later on, these guys  just sat there and
let it slide into the sea. An export award - winning company, Solid Energy, slid into
almost bankruptcy.
We wait with bated breath—bated breath—over the next few days and weeks to see
what sort of deal the Minister of Finance ha s cut with the banks to try to get rid of, or
minimise, the taxpayer’s exposure to $380 millio n worth of debt. That was all under his
watch—and all under the watch of  the Minister for State Own ed Enterprises. They are
totally, 100 percent, responsible. They get up occasionally and say they took action, and
that there is a new board in Solid Energy. Well, the problem with that proposition is that
no one got sacked. A few people resigned, no action was taken against them, and there
was no intervention by this Government.
So the poor old folks who have bought thos e shares in Mighty River Power are now
10 percent down—10 percent down. About 440,000 people pre-registered to buy those
shares. What did it work out at? One hundr ed thousand actually bought them. Opinion
polls show—I think it was the TVNZ one—that 87 percent of people do not want a bar
of Meridian Energy. And I will tell you—you look at the tele vision advertisements, you
look at the massive consultancy and legal expenses that this Government has used to try
to get these floats off the deck, and that is hundreds of millions of dollars. Yet they
baulk at the cost—which is, what, 9 milli on bucks—of a referendum on asset sales so
the people of New Zealand can actually ha ve a formal say and give this lot a good
political boot in the backside, and scuttle any moral authority they may believe they
have, through a referendum that would show they do not want their assets sold.
So John Key is quite happy to throw 30 million bucks at a multibillion-dollar,
multinational company to get—what for the taxpayer? Nothing; not even any job
security. But he is not willing to have a referendum. He criticises those who organised
that referendum, and organisations like Gr ey Power and others, and those in the
community who want to have a say. He sa ys: “No, 9 million bucks is too much.” We
support this motion, and we look forward to putting Mighty River Power’s feet to the
fire.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia Ora, Mr Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia
ora. I would like to follow on from the last member’s, Clayton Cosgrove’s, contribution.
Of course, Minister Ryall is the worst Mini ster for State Owned Enterprises that we
have seen since the whole concept was intr oduced. We have also seen one of the
shortest contributions possibly ever in our Parliament’s history with this motion. Here
you saw a Minister—blink, and you would have missed it—introducing this
Government motion No. 1 to introduce Mighty River Power as a public organisation.
The Green Party supports this motion, but we are implacably opposed to the
Government’s asset sale agenda. We believe it is important that there is public and
select committee scrutiny of Mighty River Powe r. That is why we are voting for this
motion, but we will continue to fight to our utmost in this House, on the streets, and
online to oppose the fiscally reckless, econom ically reckless, Gove rnment asset sale
agenda. The fact is that we are more focused on delivering cheaper power for Kiwis,
and a cleaner, smarter, and cheaper electricity service. We are not about flogging off the
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13793
assets and flicking them overseas. The Green  Party is supporting this motion because
we want to see Mighty River Power publicly accountable.
We saw Minister Ryall take possibly th e briefest ever ministerial contribution
introducing a Government motion to Parliament , because he is embarrassed. Of course
he is embarrassed, because he should have done this last year when the legislation was
going through Parliament. He is embarrassed because he does not want to talk about the
Government’s asset sale agenda. The Government knows it is a vote-loser. It knows that
it does not make fiscal or econom ic sense. It knows it is a lo ser plan, so it is doing its
darnedest not to talk about it. I challeng e National members to stand up and make a
contribution on this Government motion if th ey want to stand up for the asset sale
agenda.
When we are talking about this Governme nt motion, what we are seeing is Mighty
River Power being listed as a public organisa tion. Since the partial privatisation, what
we have seen is that Might y River Power is no longer a State-owned enterprise. This
means it does not come under the ambit of the traditional select committee financial
review process. By including it as a public  organisation, it will be publicly questioned
and it will be able to be included in the fi nancial review debate, because it will be a
Crown entity and a public organisation for the pu rposes of that deba te. Obviously, it is
still not able to be the subject of a request under the Official Information Act. We would
