like to see greater public transp arency, but the fact is that that highlights that Kiwis are
not in control of this State-ow ned enterprise. They are not in  control of their electricity
market. The Government would rather see the profits, the dividends, and the control
taken out of Kiwis’ hands.
The sale should not proceed. We have seen  a referendum succeed. We have seen it
pass the numbers, with 327,000 signatures. This  is a historic achievement. It is now
only the fourth petition ever to get the num bers to force a referendum. The Government
should not be pushing on. It talks about a manda te, but when it is dependent on the vote
of one man—the man, Peter D unne, who sold out our pr ivacy, sold out our human
rights laws, and is also se lling out Kiwis’ assets—it does not have a mandate. If it
wanted to put it to the test, it should wait for the referendum and listen to the voice of
New Zealanders.
This asset sale agenda just does not ma ke sense. The Government is spending
hundreds of millions of dollars  of public money on something New Zealanders do not
want. The Government cannot argue that there is a benefit for New Zealanders, and that
is clearly falling apart. What we have seen  is the value of Mighty River Power shares
plummet since the asset sale. We have seen  only 2 percent of New Zealanders being
able to pick up shares. These are not the mums and dads investors whom the ads and the
Government talk about. They are a minority of New Zealanders with the disposable
income to do it. Because of the old tax switcheroo and the Government’s fiscal
decisions, we have seen a majority of Kiwis struggling and only the top few benefiting,
and here we see public assets going to the top few for thei r benefit. It does not make
sense.
We know that the Government is unlikely to meet the original Budget forecasts of $5
billion to $7 billion. More ridiculously, what we are seeing is every New Zealand
taxpayer, even those who cannot afford to purchase shares, paying for it. We have seen
costs of more than $124 million. We have seen $2.3 million a week in forgone profit
from Mighty River Power—$2.3 million a week  forgone. And for what? For a minority
of New Zealanders who are able to afford it. That is a terrible strategy that is costing
taxpayers even more.
When we saw the—well, we did not see it  because it all happened behind closed
doors, but you can imagine the executives of Rio Tinto lick ing their lips in anticipation
13794 Standing Orders 26 Sep 2013
when the asset sale agenda  was announced, because Rio Tinto knew that it had the
Government over a barrel because of the asse t sale agenda. We saw John Key having to
negotiate with Rio Tinto from a position of weakness because of the asset sale agenda.
We saw John Key literally picking up the phone , against official advice, and giving $30
million of taxpayers’ money to Rio Tinto in T īwai because of the asset sale agenda, to
protect the asset sale agenda . The Government is doing ever ything it can, including the
fiscally reckless “buy now, pay later” scheme, which is going to cost Kiwis at least $60
million. It is time for a cup of tea. It is time  for a break. It is time for some sanity to
prevail. The Government has an opportunity with the referendum to listen to the people
of New Zealand—to put the asset sale agenda on the back-burner, have a cup of tea, and
let us re-evaluate the asset sale agenda.
The problem is, of course, that we are not  debating what we should be, which is how
we deliver cheaper power to New Zealanders . Under the asset sale agenda, what we
know is that power prices are going to go up. Under this Government—under
National—we have seen power prices go up and up by $300 a year for the average Kiwi
household. Since the Bradford reforms we have  seen our electricit y prices rise by 72
percent in real term s, while across the developed world, theirs have dropped by 6
percent. We should be having a debate about how we get cheaper electricity to New
Zealand households and New Z ealand businesses, to support  the productive sector, and
about how we get Kiwis healthy and safe a nd warm in their houses, and not in energy
poverty, which we see at the moment. By keep ing our assets in public ownership, we
could have driven cheaper and cleaner electricity.
We have a fantastic business opportunity as  a country. Our strengths are never going
to lie in competing for oil with Saudi Arabia or Venezuela. Our economic future
depends on competing on our strengths, which is clean energy, and I note that we have
actually done pretty well in a recent ranking out today. Our strengths are in innovation,
as we saw in the America’s Cup. Pricewat erhouseCoopers reckons we could see a $23
billion economic opportunity from clean ener gy. If we had kept Mighty River Power
and other State-owned ente rprise assets in public ownership, we could have
supercharged our State-owned enterprises,  coupled with private businesses, and
partnered with them to drive exports.
What we know globally is that the worl d is moving away from oil. In 2011 net
capital investment in the electricity sector —for the first time ever in our planet’s
history, fossil fuels and nucle ar energy were smaller than renewables. China, Europe,
and America are crying out for clean en ergy technology. We should not be looking to
the past, to the last century’s fossil fuel ec onomy; we should be prepared to cater to the
coming century’s economy. This is where we can build exports. It is where we can grow
jobs. We know that, compared with oil, th ere are going to be more  jobs, more profits
staying in New Zealand, and more sustainabl e prosperity for the long term in clean
energy, and that is the greatest tragedy of the asset sale agenda.
Taxpayers are forking out millions of dollars. Big multinational corporates have the
Government over a barrel, taking tens of m illions of dollars out of Kiwi taxpayers’
pockets, but we are missing the opportunity of cleaner, cheaper, and smarter energy, and
building better exports for clean energy. This is  our future and this is what the Greens
will continue to champion. We are going to fight this agenda in the House, on the
streets, and online. We will keep fighting for clean energy. Kia ora.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : Here we are again, taking  another step as a result
of the quagmire of State asset sales. The sa le of Mighty River Power Ltd was an act of
economic sabotage that will for ev er taint this Government. [ Interruption] I beg your
pardon?
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13795

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No, I was signalling to so meone behind you. I apologise
for the distraction.
DENIS O’ROURKE: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker. I will say it again. The sale
of Mighty River Power Ltd was an  act of economic sabotage that  will for ever taint this
Government and for ever damage this country’s economic and social well-being.
Everyone, except the Ministers in this Gove rnment, knows that State asset sales are
economic and financial madness. On any rational basis, they are simply barmy.
So few people support this barmy policy th at with or without a proving referendum
National is, in fact, just trashing our democrac y. It is idle nonsense to claim a mandate,
when it is abundantly obvious that this is the Governme nt’s most hated policy,
including by most of those people who voted  for National at the la st election. They did
so for reasons that are inexplicable to me, but  it is nevertheless true that they elected a
National Government knowing that National woul d sell strategic assets. They did so on
a warts and all basis. In fact, there were so  many warts that the Government’s so-called
mandate is utterly unidentifiable.
So let us hear no more talk of the Government’s claim that it now has any mandate at
all. It never really had one from the begi nning. The fundamental objection is that the
policy is now seen to be what  it really is: a swindle pe rpetrated on the public of New
Zealand. What we really own is being sold back to us—not to all of us; only some of us.
We go from assets owned by all of us to assets owned by only a few—those who can
afford to buy the shares. The result is further widening the already growing chasm
between people with the wealth and incomes for a good living and those who struggle to
earn a living, own a home, and bring up and educate their children while saving for their
retirement.
I am an egalitarian and I abhor that ki nd of swindle. A few may think they are
winners, and there may be a few pieces of silver for some, but as a nation we are
collectively impoverished by these sales. We will save the interest on some of our
borrowing in the short term, but we all lose the handsome dividend stream these
companies provide, as well as their capital growth, for the whole of our future.
To make matters worse and to exacerbate the financial stupidity of these sales, we
are paying an army of consultants and merchant  bankers a fortune to do it for us. It is a
kind of financial sadism that  we now see being imposed upon us. The total bill for the
float of Mighty River Power is a cool $41 million. That is a colossal waste of taxpayers’
money. This money would be better used el sewhere, even while this slash-and-burn
Government moves more and more to reduce the number and quality of public services
under the guise of efficiency. The Meridian Energy float is expected to cost at least
another $41 million. So that is a colossa l $82 million for absolutely nothing. That
money would be better spent on schools, hospitals, and the things that really matter.
As Brian Gaynor said in this Tuesday’s New Zealand Herald, the initial public offers
were a gravy train for the investment banks. Even Dick Turpin and the highway robbers
of old would not have been that brazen. In  fact, Dick would have been proud of the
sheer scale and audacity of these robberi es, effectively robbing the poor and middle
New Zealand to the advantage of the rich.
Although only 49 percent of th ese companies are being sold  for now, these sales are
surely only the first step of old-fashioned, true, full privatis ation in due course. This is
despite the old lessons of past privatisations  not being learnt. State asset sales of this
kind have always proved to be an unmitigated  disaster, requiring some companies to be
bought back. New Zealanders will pay a heavy price for this mad policy for generations
to come.
New Zealand’s assets are being stripped and plundered by an economically illiterate
Government that is so bereft of id eas for managing our economy prudently and
13796 Standing Orders 26 Sep 2013
effectively and without undue austerity measures that 2013 will go down as a black year
in the history of the New Zealand economy, with the sale of Mi ghty River Power and,
soon, of Meridian Energy. In the face of overwhelming economic and financial logic,
the Key Government has ploughed on with this  absurd, damaging project, regardless of
the cost to the country. National and its croni es insist on following the tried and failed
ideology of the so-called market trumping all other considera tions. The so-called
safeguards over the extent of foreign owners hip are worth as much as Mr Key’s other
bogus and empty pronouncements. He is justly regarded as our leas t trusted politician.
He is now the arch-swindler. He will go down in history as the Prime Minister who sold
out, who did dodgy deals, and he will ultimately cut and run, leaving us all to pick up
the pieces.
New Zealand First is committed to bringi ng back Mighty River Power to where it
belongs: the ownership of the people of Ne w Zealand—all of them. It is committed to
buying back State assets over time and from  the first opportunity. New Zealand First
will restore the State-owned electricity generators now being sold back into public
ownership, and will put them back under a si ngle generating entity. New Zealand First
believes in a mixed economy, one in which the private sector and the public sector work
together to provide a prosper ous and stable society that is  fair to the whole population
rather than for the benefit of only some. So although it does not oppose the principle of
transparency of information for companies such as this, New Zealand First will vote
against the motion, but only as a means of further expressing our implacable opposition
to asset sales generally.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: The Labour Party, as my
colleague the Hon Clayton Cosgrove has alr eady indicated, supports  this Government
motion No. 1 because it is one of the few ways  in which we are going to have at least a
modicum of transparency as to what is happe ning at Mighty River Power, now that half
of it is being privatised. This is necessary  only because the Government has already
taken it off the list of Stat e-owned enterprises because of the privatisation. Until that
step was taken, of course, New Zealanders  had the ability, through their members of
Parliament, to scrutinise the affairs of Mighty River Power. That was taken away
through the decision of the Government to st op it from being a State-owned enterprise
as part of the Govern ment’s programme of se lling half of the shar es. We have already
heard earlier this year from the Chief Ombuds man, Beverley Wakem, complaining that
the Government got it wrong in removing thes e companies, half of which were being
sold, from the group of entities that are c overed by the Official Information Act. She
pointed out that one of the reasons that you have transparency around these things is to
prevent cronyism and corruption.
If ever there was a Government in the history of New Zealand that is going down the
road of cronyism, which is re lated to the rise of corrupti on in democracy, it is this one.
We have seen sweet deals ne gotiated at the highest levels  of Government involving the
Prime Minister for the Skycity convention centre, for the Rio Ti nto subsidy of $30
million, which I will come back to for reasons  relating to the elec tricity market, and
then, most recently, for the intervention following the chair of Chorus phoning the
Prime Minister and complain ing about the draf t determination from the Commerce
Commission into copper broadba nd pricing for Chorus, which led to the Government
intervening for the benefit of that company.
The Chief Ombudsman was quite right in po inting out that it was wrong to remove
Mighty River Power from the list of entities th at are subject to the Official Information
Act. The excuse that was used by the G overnment—that these companies are more
commercial because they have some pr ivate shareholders—does not hold water,
because, of course, disclosure can already be refused under the Official Information Act
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13797
for matters of commercial confidentiality. So it is important that we have transparency
and openness.
I want to give another example of how , through this process of State-owned
enterprise sales, we have had too little transparency and openness. At the time of the last
election the Labour Party spot ted that the National Govern ment was promising in its
fiscal projections to sell off Government  assets—the likes of  Mighty River Power—
bank the money, and therefore not have as much borrowing and have lower interest
costs. What it did not do was account for the fact that it lost dividends and shares of
capital growth as a consequence of that sale. So it banked the savings, but it did not take
into account the lower revenue that it would have as a consequence of no longer owning
all of those companies. At the time, Steven Joyce, the master spin-doctor from the
Government, was rolled out to accuse the Labour  Party of lying and of misrepresenting.
He did that through the New Zealand Herald, he did it through the television channels,
and he went all over the radio. He got his big sword out and tried to pretend that we had
it wrong when, in fact, we were right. It was an absolute indictment on not only the
National Government and Steven Joyce that th ey were willing to misrepresent to the
people—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: They lied.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: They did. On this occasion th ey did lie to the electorate.
They lied to the electorate as to what th e fiscal effects woul d be of selling down
interests in these companies. Treasury did not force them to come clean. Treasury—in
my opinion in breach of the public finance legislation—allowed the Minister of Finance
to sign off on a set of accounts that did not show that, notwithstanding that the pre-
election fiscal update is meant, for the sake  of transparency and openness, to present a
solid set of accounts. We know that that is  necessary when you have got a National
Government, because what r eally led to that was the debacle under Mr Muldoon when
he left things in such a poor state of affairs all those years ago.
So we have had this lack of transpar ency and openness around Mighty River Power
and other share floats, we have  had the removal of them from the Official Information
Act, and now we have this little glimmer of  hope that we in the Labour Party can, at
least at the financial review, look into these accounts and critic ise them. What we
cannot do is undo what the Government is doing with these asset sales. We cannot
reverse the huge salaries and bonuses that are being paid to the chief executives of these
companies that are being floated, which increas e the costs that have to be charged to
power consumers. We cannot change the fact that mone y has been wasted on the
process—many hundreds of millions of dollars  in terms of advice and commissions
being paid on sale.
We ought not to forget that this is centr al to the National Government’s economic
agenda for these 3 years, even though it is  opposed by so many New Zealanders, yet it
does nothing to improve New Zealand’s economic output. Changing who owns what
already exists does not change how much electricity is produced; all it does is put up the
price. The Government is always telling us “Look, we’ve got a co mpetitive electricity
market that constrains price.”, and yet we know that New Zeal anders do not believe
that, because it is not true. We know that  New Zealand’s electricity prices have
increased at twice the rate of inflation for about 20 years. We know that the differential
between residential, and commercial and indus trial, tariffs is the second-highest in the
developed world after Denmark, and cannot be  properly explained except by a lack of
competition. We have even in the last few weeks had another intervention by the
Government, in respect of the Meridian Energy share sale, to get Meridian Energy off
the block. It did a deal with the owners of the Tīwai Point smelter. It gave a $30 million
subsidy, effectively for the bene fit of Rio Tinto, in order to  give certainty  to Meridian
13798 Standing Orders 26 Sep 2013
Energy that it would still be able  to sell its power at inflated prices and keep the prices
high. We know that Treasury advised that but for that intervention, the price of
electricity could have decr eased for everyone by 10 per cent. Yet the Government
pretends that we have got a competitive electricity market.
I just find it absolutely incredible that we have not had outrage from investment
bankers because of this market interventi on by the Government, which proved that the
electricity market was not competitive. But the reason we have not had outrage from
that quarter is, of course, that they are se lf-interested in keeping the existing so-called
market model. It is certainly not a comp etitive market model; it is an uncompetitive
market model. They are self-interested becau se they want to clip the ticket on these
sales. They like the privatisation of these assets. They are some of those who benefit
from the sell-down of these assets to the less than 3 percent of the New Zealand
population who owns what was previously wholly New Zealand - owned.
This programme on the part of the Government is wrong. We do support this motion.
We do not think that the Government should be given much credit for it, because, of
course, whilst it is doing this—which is the absolute minimum it can do—it is running
roughshod over the will of New Zealanders. Citizens initiated referenda are provided for
under the constitutional arrangements of New Zealand. When a citizens initiated
referendum is brought forward and the more than 300,000 signatures that are needed to
cross that hurdle are obtained, and if there is  no urgency to proceed in respect of the
issue that was so contentious—and there is no urgency to proceed with the likes of the
Meridian Energy sale—a prudent Governme nt would just wait and see what the
referendum turns up.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Respect the people.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: You would respect the peop le, and you would give due
consideration to the outcome of that referendum. This arrogant Government, of course,
is just ignoring the will of th e people, pretending that it has got a mandate for this when
it has not, ignoring the fact that it makes the finances of the Government worse,
ignoring the fact that it incr eases the gap between the rich  and the poor, ignoring the
fact that it makes the economy go slower if you have got a higher electricity price—
because businesses are not as competitiv e and they cannot employ as many people—
and ignoring the fact that it ha s an adverse effect on the w ealth of the country because
you do not have as many exports and you import more stuff instead if your energy price
is higher than it need be. The Government  is doing all of that because of this
ideologically driven nonsense of selling these shares in not just Mighty River Power but
also Meridian Energy. So although the Labour Party supports this motion, let that not be
confused with giving any support for this ridi culous central part of the Government’s
economic agenda.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Labour will be supporting this Government motion,
and we will be doing so because, as my colleague David Parker said, it is one of the few
protections that are going to remain to ensure transparency around the operation of what
used to be State-owned enterprises, power companies—one power company, in
particular, Mighty River Power, which used to be wholly owned by the people of New
Zealand and has now been partially priv atised by a Government running roughshod
over public concern and public opposition to asset sales. So although we remain firmly
opposed to the asset sales ag enda of this Government, we do support this motion
because it will mean that Mighty River Powe r would still be able to participate, for
example, in financial reviews and will come under the Standing Orders of this House.
But I think this motion really highlights what a complete stuff-up the Government’s
asset sales programme has been. The Governme nt seems to be in some kind of blind
panic. It has no other plan. It is creating a slush fund that it promised would be for
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13799
schools and hospitals, and which turns out is  for any old thing. The Government had
spent the money in the Budget before the mone y had even come in. This is despite the
fact that the original prediction for how ma ny billions of dollars would be brought in
from the sale of these energy assets has b een substantially reduced and reviewed. The
reality has been that the money the Govern ment was expecting has not been made and
yet it was already budgeted for and spent. That  is obviously a concer n for this side of
the House, because we are going to be picking up the Government books in 2014.
Once again, we are going to have a Labour Government that comes in and sorts out
the utter, utter economic mess left behind by a National Government completely devoid
of any real economic development ideas and completely devoid of any kinds of ideas
that are going to grow our economy in a sustainable way and produce real jobs,
environmentally and economically sustainable jobs. Instead, it is just another fire sale of
assets that are critical to the economic and environmental well-being of our country.
Mighty River Power is a good example of th is because it is a world leader in
geothermal energy. It is able to take the intellectual property that it owns as a company,
borne out of many, many years of developi ng geothermal energy options in New
Zealand, and use that to assist other countries, particularly countries that are seismically
active. We have seen, with the tragedy in  Japan, what can happen with nuclear power
plants in seismically active parts of the world. But where there is seismic activity, there
is often geothermal activity. Mighty River Power obviously has an enormous amount of
potential in that area. That is potential th at the taxpayers of New Zealand could have
fully benefited from had we kept the company in public ownership, and had we kept the
dividends that will come from these activit ies being carried out by Mighty River Power
in public hands and in the public coffers held by the Government.
We are here doing this because of the rush, because of the panic, and because of the
complete stuff-up in how this asset sales programme has gone ahead. It is a fairly
significant oversight by the Government that when it passed legislation and when it was
removing Mighty River Power’s stat us as a State-owned enterpri se, it forgot to give it
the new status of a public organisation. That is a fairly large oversight, but it tells you
just how rushed these processes have been.
We saw that again with the $30 m illion subsidy that was given to T īwai Point. The
Government says that it did that because it  was all about protecti ng jobs. My colleague
Clayton Cosgrove then asked whether the G overnment made keeping jobs or retaining
those jobs a requirement of that $30 milli on. He asked whether the Government had
said that in order to get that $30 million th e company had to guarantee that the jobs will
be retained. No—no, the Government just hand ed over the cheque and said: “There you
go. Have a good time. Thank you very much.” [ Interruption] Absolutely. I know. It is
astounding—$30 million, and no guarantee was even asked for.

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: Just a handout.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Just a handout. The Governme nt did not even say: “Would
you please consider keeping these jobs.”
There is another side to that argument , about the irony of a National Government
subsidising jobs, which it would always rail against but now seems to think is a great
idea. But now we have a handing over of $30 million, which is meant to save jobs but
will not because there was no guarantee of those jobs being saved.
That shows the desperation in this Gove rnment to force through this asset sales
regime—the utter desperation that it woul d get in there, give a major multinational
company $30 million, and then not even ask that the basic requirement of keeping
people in work be adhered to by the compa ny getting the corporate bailout. That is
utterly shameful—utterl y shameful—but the Government is so obsessed with firming
up Meridian Energy, which is the next one off the blocks to be sold off, so utterly
13800 Standing Orders 26 Sep 2013
obsessed with firming it up for sale, that it  will do anything, absolutely anything. And
guess what, taxpayers of New Zealand? Th e Government will spend your money to do
it.
Now when you ask for your local health se rvices to be reta ined and to be
strengthened, if you want your rail line fixed or reopened after a washout, or if you want
more money for your local school, well, gue ss what, voters of Ne w Zealand? You are
not going to get that. But if you are a multinational company that can help with the asset
sales regime, here is $30 million—easy as pie. Done. You do not even have to ask
twice. That is the kind of corporate cr onyism that we have under this National-led
Government.
One of the reasons why it is so utterly important that we  do maintain the ability for
scrutiny of these companies at select committe es is the concern that Labour has raised
over the impact on power prices caused by this  privatisation regime of the Government,
because power prices will go up. They will go  up. These are very efficient companies.
That is why the Government is selling them  off. And when those companies no longer
have to consider the social impacts of wh at they do, as they do under the State-Owned
Enterprises Act, when they are no longer constrained by that, and when they have
private shareholders who want to get maximu m value out of their shares, what are they
going to do? Well, they are going to put up power prices. And can they do it? Of course
they can, because it is a completely unregulated environment—completely unregulated.
So we have the National Government desper ately trying to claim that power prices
have gone up because of lines charges. Well, that  is not true. Or it is trying to claim that
they have gone up because of Transpower nati onal grid charges. Well, that is true but
only because the National Government reversed the decision of the former Labour
Government, which said: “Yes, Transpower, you  have to upgrade the national grid. Our
economy depends on it. But guess what? We are going to forgo your dividend to pay for
it. So there is no pass-through cost to consumers, because you will be able to pay for it
out of your dividend.”
What did National do? As soon as it was elected—well, one, it did continue with
that asset upgrade programme; that is good. Bu t, two, it said to Transpower: “Sorry, we
want a dividend, and can you please back pay us  for the dividends that you did not pay
to the Labour Government.” So that is pushing up power prices. That is the direct result
of this National Government.
The problem we have is that in the reta il market we do not have competition—we do
not. The question that I put to the Government—it goes on and on about its What’s My
Number campaign, and the amount of money it has been putting into that. Well, if we
have a really competitive market, why do we need a What’s My Number campaign?
Why do we need a Government campaign to he lp people find cheaper electricity prices
if we have a truly competitive electricity market? The reality is that we do not.
I question the effectiveness of the What ’s My Number campaign because for the
poorest people they are lucky if they can find one power company to pick them up. The
idea that they have the choice  of electricity providers is  utter fantasyland stuff and
shows how out of touch this Government is. The other reason that I am sceptical about
that programme is that not only do you have to have access to the internet in order to be
able to get on there and check it out but a lot of the savings are actually down to early
payment discounts, not cheaper electricity prices. If you cannot pay your bill at all, then
an early payment discount is not going to help you.
The What’s My Number campaign has not he lped the people in this country who are
struggling the most to pay power bills. Wh at will help them is Labour’s NZ Power
policy, which will ensure that we have co mpetition in the retail  market. We are not
going to be regulating the retail  market. What we are going to be doing is ensuring an
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13801
actual competitive market so that consumers will have choice, and so that more players
will be able to enter into that market and develop scale, because that is what does not
happen at the moment. We have a lot of sm all players. The big four are happy to let
them stay there and give the appearance of competition, but the moment they got to any
scale they would squash them. The moment  those companies had so many connections
that they would start to have to hedge, th at is when the generator-retailers really
exercise their power over the electricity market.
So the kind of reform that the Labour Party has been talking about is the only kind of
reform that is going to make a difference to  power prices. It has been because of the
Government’s asset sales agenda, because of the loss of control of those State-owned
enterprises that we saw, that we had to a nnounce that we were go ing to be doing this.
Now was the time. We have flattening demand, we have surplus of supply, and we have
a power sector that formerly was 75 pe rcent owned by the New Zealand public now
being partially privatised, lo sing that transparency, and lo sing that ability to protect
consumers in New Zealand. That meant that the time for electricity reform has come,
and a Labour Government in 2014 will do that. We do support this Government motion,
but we utterly oppose the premise upon which it is based.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I want to take a brief call on this
Government motion No. 1, as well.  It is pretty extraordinary that we have got to this
point, where we have to pass this today b ecause it was forgotten to have been done
some time before. It is easy to forget accoun tability, really, is it not? At the end of the
day, it is just about whether we can keep a check on Mighty River Power and our other
power organisations. It is also a bit of a j oke to actually put this under the category of a
public organisation, because it cer tainly is not a public orga nisation any more. It was,
but now it really is a priva tised organisation and not a public organisation, because
Mighty River Power is half-owned by just 2 percent of New Zealand’s population. The
rest of New Zealand, the other 98 percent, were not able to take a share in Mighty River
Power. So now we have Mighty River Po wer, which is worth $2.25 a share but was
floated at $2.50 a share. It has gone down 10 percent already, and wh at a failure of an
investment that has been for that 2 percent of the population who has joined in that.
On the basis of that success, of that br illiant move by this Government, we are now
going to float an even bigger power organisa tion, Meridian Energy. So we have failed
on Mighty River Power, and now we are going to launch off Meridian Energy. Who
will invest in Meridian Energy? Well, 34 percent of people said before Mighty River
Power was floated that they would invest in  Mighty River Power, and it ended up being
2 percent. When the pollsters asked New Z ealanders this time about Meridian Energy,
only 14 percent said that they were going to  invest in Meridian Energy. Obviously, this
caused some panic amongst the Government, b ecause it then started acting a little bit
like Harvey Norman—buy now, pay later. So yo u are able to buy those shares now and
pay later. As my colleague Clayton Cosgr ove says, they will throw in a box of steak
knives along with it just to sweeten the deal up a bit. They will probably offer a trip for
two to Las Vegas, where you coul d have the same sort of gamble but more legally over
there. This is to try to get this float across the line.
What will we get for the money? Well, we were promised $7 billion to $10 billion,
then it was $5 billion to $7 billion, then it was the low end of $5 billion to $7 billion—
and these are all quotes of either the Mini ster of Finance or the Prime Minister—and
now we are scratching to get $5 billion across the line. What  will we spend that money
on? Well, there has been a wide variety of issues that we can spend this money on. First
of all, of course, it was to avoid the cr edit downgrade—avoid that. That was in 2011. I
do not suppose people remember  that. Then it was to help  Kiwibank. Then in 2012 it
was to pay down debt. That was Mr Ryall’s suggestion. Then it was to build new
13802 Standing Orders 26 Sep 2013
schools and hospitals. That did the rounds for a while because it was very popular. And
then it was to bail out KiwiRail. Then it was to  irrigate lots and lots of farm land, a little
bit like the Tukituki River, which we are hearing so much about. What an appalling idea
that is. It is so appalling that the Government has to doctor the results of its tests in
order to be able to get it across the line. Then it is the rebuild of Christchurch. Then it is
the Auckland rail loop. The list goes on and on. If you add it up, it comes to $80 billion.
So the $5 billion being raised goes into $80 billion. I am not sure how that works.
What I do know is that the mums and dads who were promised the shares in this are
a joke; it is just 2 percent of our population. We will not get anything like what we want
for the power companies, and, as my collea gue Moana Mackey just said, power prices
will go up. We lose all the way down the line,  unless you are in that 1 percent and 2
percent upper-income level. This is a disgr ace, and this Government motion No. 1 is a
testament to that.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. Talofa. The
question today is whether Mighty River Power should be a public organisation. That is a
most obvious no-brainer—of course Mighty Ri ver Power should be subject to scrutiny.
It must be subject to pub lic scrutiny. It cannot  be exempt from public scrutiny. The
mums and dads who have been led astray by the National Party ar e deserving of some
protection; heaven knows there is none for them in the sh aremarket. If you compare the
reaction of that Government to the equity of mum and da d investors—and that is the
Government’s term, its sneering way of refe rring to the poor peop le of New Zealand;
poor in both senses of the word now. Th e poor people did thei r dough in Mighty River
Power at $2.50.
Compare the reactions of Sam Lotu -Iiga and the Hon Peter Dunne on The Vote on
TV a fortnight ago, where they nearly became hysterical over the equity that speculators
have in the housing bubble. Those two memb ers attacked the O pposition stridently.
They shouted that we were going to destroy the equity that speculators have in their
housing portfolios—with 50, 100, 200 residential properties in their portfolios—and not
a word, not an ounce, of sympathy from Pete r Dunne and Sam Lotu-Iiga for the first-
home buyers, the young families who have no way to accumulate wealth under this
Government’s policies, nor from anyone else in the National Government.
Yet what has happened to the Mighty Rive r Power share price? It has gone down,
down, down, faster than a skydiver, and there is no parachute. Since listing in mid-May,
over $400 million of wealth has been destroyed. From an issue price of $2.50 a share, in
4 short months it has dropped to $2.23, and ju st 10 days ago it reac hed an all-time low
of $2.16. Looking at the trend he re, there is no bottom in sight. Mighty River Power
share price fluctuations are on a downward trend. The shares have lost over 13 percent
in value over just 4 short months, and at this rate mum and dad investors will have lost
half their money within the year and will have done their dough totally by mid-2015.
Maybe that does not worry Bill English because  he is gambling on th at being after the
next election.
John Key is flogging off Mighty River Power and the other State-owned enterprises
like the family silver. We have seen a numb er of questionable manoeuvres from this
Government—financial dealings that really  are little different from Bridgecorp or
Hanover Finance. It moves power statio ns around between Mighty River Power and
Meridian Energy and Genesis like the pea in  a three-card shell game. The hard-working
folks at the Tekap ō A, Tekap ō B, and Whirinaki power stations could be excused for
not knowing who owned each power station on a particular day.
With Meridian Energy, our next State-owned enterprise to be so ld, we have seen a
$30 million handout to Rio Tinto. But what is not being told about that story is the
absolute incompetence of the Minister fo r State Owned Enterprises—asleep at the
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13803
wheel, because who could not see Rio Tint o manoeuvring New Zealand? Fancy that
Minister allowing Rio Tinto to manoeuvre New Zealand into such a vulnerable position.
It would be very interesti ng to have the disi nfectant of sunlight looking at the
relationship between the heads of Comalc o, those National Party cronies, and the
Minister for State Owned Enterprises.
We now have Bill English thinking we are very gullible. He is, sadly, banking on the
adage that there is one born every minute. We come along with a “buy now, pay later”
deal, as my colleagues have stressed, and steak knives, and people get to keep 100
percent of the dividend, when they have not ac tually paid for the shares. But wait, there
is more. He has set a price cap on the shares so that his few mates who can afford to buy
them can get in at a lower price than they should. And let us not forget the $100 million
or so paid to Aussie banks just to prepare for the float. The prices that these are going to
be sold for represent another subsidy from the hard-working families of New Zealand—
the people whose power prices are going to go up and up just to support a few.
It is interesting that Bill English ignored  Treasury. He ignored Treasury’s advice
against it. To Treasury’s credit, it did warn  Bill English and John Key that the emperor
has no clothes. This motion represents a small step to turn back the tide, to expose what
ongoing mischief there may be from Nati onal over this power company, which the
public built up over 80 years. It used to be the jewel in our crown. It is a public asset of
benefit to the public, which this Government is selling off.
Motion agreed to.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I move, That the following
sessional order be adopted: “Standing Order 140(3)  to be read subject to the following
additional order: ‘(d) with permission granted  by the Speaker to be absent on account
of illness or other family cause of a personal nature following a request from a
member’s party leader or whip.’”

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I rise in support of Government
motion No. 2. I was expecting the Government to perhaps enlarge on the reasons behind
the motion, but perhaps it is not entirely sure . I want to actually formally thank the
Speaker for taking notice of some situations  that certainly Labour members have found
themselves in. Newsflash, to people who might be watching this: we are human, and
just like other people in their workplaces we sometimes have family situations and
illnesses that prevent us from being able to take up our work in the way that we would
wish to take it up.
The point of this motion is that it allows  compassionate leave to be put in place so
that if one of our MPs from any party in this  Parliament is in that  situation, then their
party is not penalised by having their vote not  count in certain ci rcumstances. That will
be monitored very closely and stringently by the party whips and that is important.
I frequently, in my role as a female member of Parliament, travel the country, talking
to lots of people, many of whom are wome n, about the importance of having women in
Parliament. It is important, therefore, that we make sure that it is a working environment
in which women can operate, and that means,  yes, recognising that we have family
circumstances that are beyond our control sometimes. Some of the situations that
members have found themselves in—perhaps the public are wondering what on earth
this compassionate leave could possibly be  about in a parliamentary environment.
Examples that come to mind are examples such as that suffered by a very good friend
the Hon Vui Mark Gosche, when his wife was very ill for a period of time. Of course
we would want him to be able to support his wife and his family members at that time,
and that is the type of occasion that this motion will help with.
13804 Standing Orders 26 Sep 2013
It does mean that when family members have taken ill, or in situations where
children or dependent family members are i ll, we too can respond to that as other
members of the public could in their own wo rk environments. And it means that we
would actually have a voting system in place to make sure that a party’s vote is not
affected by that.
Without any further ado, I welcome this Government motion No. 2. I thank the
Speaker, in particular, for taking this issue se riously, because if we are truly going to be
a House of Representatives, then we do need to make sure that a whole range of people,
no matter their family circumstances, can take part in being a member of Parliament and
take part in the debate in this place. Thank you.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. Ng ā
mihi nui ki a koutou. I rise on behalf of the Green Party to support this Government
motion No. 2 introducing a draft sessional or der for a new category of leave called
compassionate leave. This Chamber is not noted for its compassion. It is more noted for
its dog-eat-dog, political, partisan, petty poin t-scoring. It is not known for its family-
friendly work hours. It is not known for the camaraderie or for the collaborative,
positive process. But it is great that this Parliament, on the last day of this session, is
also debating this motion to see a new categ ory, compassionate leave. I think everyone
in this Parliament would like to see a bit more compassion in this debating chamber.
When it comes to the issue of leave, th ere are two mechanisms that members and
their parties can go through to de al with this issue. The firs t is under the discretion of
the Speaker and relates to th e Civil List Act 1979, which relates to our remuneration.
The second one, which the public might be more  familiar with, is the issue of leave for
MPs to be able to leave the parliamentary pr ecincts but for their vote to be cast. At the
moment, parties can have 25 percent of their members away without dropping down
their votes.
I think many people—and I know I get a number of messages online and emails
about it—constantly ask why there are so few people in this debating chamber. The
answer, of course, is not that all the MPs are off bunking or down at the pub—at the
Back Bencher. The fact is that many MP s are out doing constituency work, at
community functions, or, in fact, are hard at work in their offices. Under the MMP
environment, party votes are cast by the party, not by the individual, so whips—or
musterers, as we call them in the Green Party—have the discretion to allow MPs to
have leave.
What we have not had is the ability for Pa rliament to have a new category of leave
called compassionate leave. At the moment, regardless of what the purpose of the leave
is—be it that the MP is sick, on family duties, or has any other personal issue—it comes
out of that party’s entitlement. This has the perverse incentive for those MPs who
maybe have a family, personal, or health issue not to apply for leave, because they
might be disadvantaging their colleagues w ho may be spending time at a function or
speaking at a conference. The message that we do not want to send is that sick MPs
should stay working at Parliament so their colleagues can have leav e at conferences or
out campaigning.
What we want to have is a safe work  environment where if MPs have health
problems or family problems or family issues, they should be able to take leave. It is
great to see this. It is something the Gr een Party has been pushing for on the Business
Committee. I would like to acknowledge the work of Holly Walker, who, facing an
imminent birth of her own, has been drivi ng this. I am not awar e that her birth has
occurred. She has not updated Twitter for about 7 hours, so hopefully she is not going
into labour as we speak.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: What’s her due date?
26 Sep 2013 Standing Orders 13805

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: I am not sure of her due date. It must be pretty soon.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Five days ago.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Five days ago was her due date, so I am sure this Parliament
will be eagerly waiting for the news of Holly’s baby’s birth.
As the member Sue Moroney points out, wh at we want to have is a House of
Representatives that is truly representative , including of young parents. As a father to
two young kids, aged 3 and 6, it is a struggl e to be a good dad and a good member of
Parliament. It is great to see Parliament coming together with this new amendment to
Standing Order 140(3) that allows the Speaker to grant this new category of
compassionate leave.
I have two quick points on this. The Greens w ould like to see this entrenched in the
Standing Orders, not just in a temporary sessional order. We want to see it entrenched.
We want to see a compassiona te Parliament with compassionate leave in the rule book.
We want to see the issue of parental leave distinctly added. At the moment, it is only
compassionate leave. We think parental le ave is important. Looking after your kids and
supporting your whānau is important.
It is just one of many Standing Orders ch anges the Green Party wants to see. I will
soon be putting in a submission from the Gr eens. We have got around 17 substantive
points where we can modernise our parliame ntary rules and where we can have better
legislative lawmaking—for example, in te rms of substantive amendments, which the
Government has been using a great deal of , to circumvent the New Zealand Bill of
Rights Act and select committee scrutiny. These points go through to lobbying changes,
through to international treaty  provisions, through to the election of the Speaker, and
through to something close to my heart, which is reforming the issue of the prayer.
What we are seeing here with the compassi onate leave changes is Parliament slowly
modernising and becoming a more family-friendly, a more personal, health, and well-
being - friendly, and a more compassionate place. There is a long way to go. This is just
the start, and the Green Party will keep being the party that is proposing positive
solutions to support members and to suppor t the lawmaking process in New Zealand.
We will keep making these positive solutions  and supporting them when they are in
front of this House. Kia ora.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: On behalf of New Zealand First, I rise
to take a very short call on Government mo tion No. 2, which relate s to Standing Order
140(3). I think it is fair to say that from time to time unf oreseen circumstances arise
when members of Parliament do need to be absent from the parlia mentary precincts on
compassionate grounds and do need to be rega rded as if they were present for the
purposes of casting party votes.
Potentially, there is a wide range of contingencies that may fall under this provision.
It is neither practical nor appropriate to  describe in elaborate detail what these
circumstances may be. In our view, it is ap propriate that the provisions Parliament
makes for such circumstances—compassionate grounds—reflect and are consistent with
the modern world and the approaches that ar e adopted in the world of work outside of
these four walls. We are satisfied that th e procedure envisaged in this motion will
actually meet that test. We do not consider th at these provisions are excessive or create
significant or unwanted privil eges for parliamentarians. New Zealand First considers
that what is proposed is a practical and appropriate measure, and we support the motion.
Motion agreed to.
13806 Administration of Community Se ntences and Orders Bill 26 Sep 2013

sections.heading: Administration Of Community Sentences And Orders Bill

items.text: In Committee

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I seek leave for there to be a
single debate on the bill, with all questions put separately at the end of the debate.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is there
any objection? There is no objection.
Parts 1 to 4, clauses 1 and 2

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I want to take just a few
moments at the beginning of this bill, th e Administration of Co mmunity Sentences and
Orders Bill, and then I know  that colleagues around the Chamber will make some
further comments. Although this bill is genera lly concerned with matters of a technical
or administrative nature, I do believe that th e cumulative effect of the amendments will
be a considerable improvement in the overa ll management of community sentences and
orders. For instance, the bill contributes to the goal of improving public safety by better
aligning electronic monitoring conditions with electronic boundari es of monitoring
equipment, making it easier to hold offenders to account if they fail to comply with a
community-based sentence, and it does addre ss some technical problems with extended
supervision order provisions.
The bill also reduces the administrative burden that probation officers face and
empowers them in other ways to focus more on the rehabilitative opportunities available
to offenders and on the safety of the public. For example, they will be able to approve
basic work and living skills courses for of fenders on community work, without having
to apply to the court. A small technical change like that can make an enormous
difference in the life of the offenders, as it sa ves all that bureaucratic hassle that they go
through, and also make it a better job for our probation officers. We have done some
technical tidy-ups around ambi guous provisions, or some of the provisions that have
had unintended consequences. But overall this bill is designed to significantly improve
the effective administration of sentences and orders in the community, both for the
officers and also for the offenders.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Thank you very much for the opportunity to
speak in the Committee stage of the Admi nistration of Community Sentences and
Orders Bill. We on this side  of the Chamber find ourselves  in the not too unfamiliar
position of supporting the Government on this piece of legislation.
As the Minister of Corrections said, this bill is about improving the effectiveness of
sentences that are served in the community, and I think we will find over time that we
will be encouraging, where appropriate, sentences to be served in the community, for a
couple of reasons. The first reason is that th ere is evidence that those offenders who
have the opportunity to serve their sentences at home have a lower recidivism rate than
those who serve their sentences inside a pris on—I will be able to talk in much detail
about that—and the second re ason is, obviously, a fiscal one. We simply cannot
continue to lock people up for long periods of time given the fiscal constraints we have
at the moment.
As the Deputy Prime Minister has already pointed out, our prison system is both a
moral and a fiscal failure. We simply cannot afford to let the leve l of expenditure, the
track the Department of Corrections is on, continue. Making sure we are being much
more effective with our spending and w ith our rehabilitati on of people who are
sentenced is something that I think people on all sides of this Chamber would want.
I thank the submitters who gave evidence to the Law and Order Committee. This is a
select committee that, unfortunately, I no l onger have the pleasure of being on. I
26 Sep 2013 Administration of Commun ity Sentences and Orders Bill 13807
acknowledge the chair of the se lect committee, Jacqui Dean, who has just walked into
the Chamber, for the way in which this bill was handled during the select committee
process. There were some odder moments during the select committee process when we
were told about the difference between a sq uare and a circle for the purpose of the
electronic monitoring of pe ople who are on home detention. For those who are
wondering about that and how that may work, if someone is on electronic monitoring at
home, the signal that is sent to  the box, essentially to make su re that they stay at that
residence, is an electronic si gnal that is very much a circ le. But there could be a patch
outside that residence where that circle doe s emanate out to, so technically they could
be within the electronic zone of their monitoring but technically outside the address—
Simon O’Connor: Is this Euclidean geometry or non-Euclidean geometry?

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Do not ask me those kinds of que stions, please. Technically they
could be outside the address where they were meant to be, but the electronic monitoring
would not be able to pick that up. So ther e were some interesting moments during the
select committee process, and certainly some of those technicalities were ironed out.
I have mentioned the rates of recidivism fo r offenders who served their sentences in
the community and for offenders who went to prison. There was a submission during
the select committee process from the Salvati on Army, and I would like just to refer to
that now. It quoted some 2009 Ministry of Ju stice figures that said the ministry had
found that 23 percent of those on home de tention in 2009 were reconvicted in the 12
months after they served their sentence. But, conversely, 52.6 percent of those who
served a custodial sentence in 2009 were reconvicted in the following 12 months. So
there is certainly hard data from the Ministry  of Justice that suggests that offenders who
serve their sentence at home have a much better chance of not reoffending. The
numbers are quite stark: 23 percent of those who serve a sentence of home detention are
reconvicted of a crime in the 12 months after they have served thei r sentence, and 52.6
percent of those who serve a sentence inside a prison went on to reoffend.
So there is good, hard evidence as to why we should be investing much more time
and energy in making sure we are much more efficient and effective in terms of home
detention sentences. Certainly there are some people who should be serving their
sentences in a prison; they cannot be trusted to be in the community when they are
serving those sentences. I thi nk those numbers also bear th at out. But for those who do
have the privilege—and I guess it is a privil ege—of serving their sentence within our
communities, the recidivism rate is much, much lower, and we should give the credit
where credit is due and make sure the comm unity sentence regime is much, much more
effective.
There was a range of views at the select committee about whether or not there should
be more investment in our prison service. Bu t I think that on this side of the Chamber
we would certainly like to see more focus on community sentences and more
investment in rehabilitation services as well. That is not to say that there is not good
work going on within our prison service on re habilitation. There certainly is good stuff
going on there, and the Chairperson, Lindsay Tisch, was, I think, part of the Law and
Order Committee that visited some prisons where we saw some very good work. That
was very starkly shown in some of the drug treatment units ar ound the country, where
there is some very good intense work going on, not just by prison staff but by outside
agencies, to make sure that these people—a nd these are hardened drug users who are in
our prison service—are getting very intense drug treatment, as well as support after they
finish their prison sentences.
If there is one thing that I think we should be making mu ch of a priority it is
wrapping around services for those inmates who have gone through a 3-month—I think
it is—course in these drug treatment units in  our prisons. They are released into the
13808 Administration of Community Se ntences and Orders Bill 26 Sep 2013
community after they have served  their sentences, and we rea lly need to make sure that
the investment we have made in them while they are in prison does not go to waste
when we release them. Many of them will go back into the same communities and the
same situations, and some will put themselves into situations that are very similar to
those that got them into troubl e in the first place, and we do not want to see a huge
waste of time, energy, and aroha, I guess you could say—because some of these drug
treatment courses are very much focused around Māori culture.
We need to make sure we are getting good bang for buck out of the drug treatment
units and other treatments we are putting these inmates through, and we need to make
sure we wrap services round them after they leave prison. Of course, there is a danger to
that, because some will say: “We should ju st let them go. They have served their
sentence, and we don’t care about them; they  are people who have broken the law.” But
if we are going to make an investment in these people and try to get them back on the
straight and narrow—off the dr ugs, off the alcohol, and into a place where they are not
reoffending—we need to make sure we are supporting them in our communities. That
means fewer victims. That is what everyone in this Chamber would want, and that is
why we should be making sure that there is much more intense post-release support for
a lot of these people who are going through drug treatment units.
Just before I conclude, I go back to the usefulness of community sentences, which
we are debating here in this bill. As I have said a couple of times now, the recidivism
rate—it is not an easy word to say fa st—of those people who serve community
sentences is almost, if not, half that of t hose who serve prison sentences. It should be
something that we as a country should look  to do much, much more about in cases
where it is possible and safe to do so becau se it has been proved that people who serve
community sentences do not reoffend as much as those who serve a prison sentence. It
also gives the ability for those people to st ill be integrated with in their community and
to still be supported by their families or support people in the community, and I think
that is something that we should look to do much, much more in order to help
rehabilitate these offenders.
Of course, there is a fiscal argument to this  as well. It is much, much cheaper. Of the
$4 billion that is spent in the justice sector, I believe that about 30 percent of it is spent
on corrections. It is $1.2 billi on, and that will grow if we do not do anything about it.
We must do something about it. Community  sentences are certainly one way to do
something about it. The rehabilitation aspe ct works, we make sure there is less
reoffending and fewer victims, and the penni es are watched too—because there is $1.2
billion of taxpayer money going into the correction system. So Labour does support this
piece of legislation. It makes the community se ntences much more efficient, and that is
why we will continue to support it.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I am very happy to speak to the Committee
of the whole House stage of the Administ ration of Community Sentences and Orders
Bill. I want to thank the Minister of Corrections, Anne Tolley, for bringing this bill to
Parliament and continuing the work of the National Government in providing efficiency
within our corrections servic e. And why does that matter? Why is it so important to
improve on efficiency? It is because in doing that, we will hopefully have better
outcomes, not only for the prisoners going thro ugh our corrections system and/or on to
community sentences but by aiding in the rate of non-reoffending. We do not want to
see again people who go through our corrections  system. We do not want to see them
again experiencing community services. So th e more this Government can do to make
the administration of the systems around correct ions more efficient, then, hopefully, the
better the outcome we will have.
26 Sep 2013 Administration of Commun ity Sentences and Orders Bill 13809
When the Hon Anne Tolley introduced this bi ll to the House and gave it to the care
of the Law and Order Committee, she made it very clear that that was her aim, and that
her desire was that in impr oving the systems, we would improve the outcomes. Already
we have seen a drop in crime. We have s een a drop in youth crime. All the trends are
going the right way in the corrections system and in the justice system, and this piece of
legislation continues that good work. Two bills were introduced to the House to remove
barriers to the efficiency and the effectiv eness of the administration of corrections
sentences and community sentences. The comm ittee and the House ha ve dealt with the
Corrections Amendment Bill. That part of th e work relates to prisons and corrections,
and that was passed through the House last month. Now we are moving in a timely
manner with the Administration of Community Sentences and Orders Bill. That is the
bill we are addressing today.
What this bill does is amend the Bail Act, the Parole Act, and the Sentencing Act.
These Acts play a large part in the govern ing and administration of sentences and of
orders in our communities through our corrections system. The introduction of extended
supervision orders—and that happened in  2004—and of sentencing and parole reforms
in late 2007 left some procedures for ma naging offenders in the community rather
unclear. The previous speaker, Kris Faafoi—whom I want to thank for his work on the
Law and Order Committee, and express my regret that he has moved on to another
select committee, because he did make wort hwhile contributions, worked collegially
when it was appropriate, and asked the tough  questions when it was appropriate—did
point out in his intervention that a community sentence with a GPS might be described
as a circle on an offender’s  property. Previously, if the mailbox was just outside that
circle, the offender would be going against their community sentence if they walked out
to the mailbox to get the mail, or chased the cat, or something like that. So there were
anomalies that were easily identified. We ha ve sought, through this legislation, to make
the measures around community sentences more pragmatic, more workable, more
efficient, and more helpful, not only to  the probation service but to the prisoners
themselves. This bill provides clarificati on, and it introduces a number of minor policy
changes to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of home detention, community-
based sentences, and also the new electronic monitoring regime.
I just want to talk a little bit about th e probation service. As a part of our
investigation into this bill, we went out  to Lower Hutt and met with the probation
service and heard about the work it is doing with community sentences. It struck me
what a long way our corrections system and our whole justice sector have come in such
a short time, in the desire for a good, str ong, rehabilitative appro ach to reintegrating
prisoners out of the corrections system th rough community sentences, if that is the
pathway, or through just community sentences— reintegrating them back into society in
the best shape, so that they can go out, ha ve good lives, get a job, have skills, and not
return back through the loop, knocking on the door  of the District Court and going back
into the corrections system, just to waste another part of their lives. This is a good bill. I
congratulate the Minister. I thank the select  committee, and I commend the bill to the
House.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First): Today I rise on behalf of
New Zealand First to speak to the Administ ration of Community Sentences and Orders
Bill at its Committee stage. I think we all agree that law and order is very important to
our country. It is crucial not only to maintain order in our society but also to ensure
safety and maximise security for all New Zealanders. We are all aware that some of our
citizens continue to break the law, some fail to behave in accordance with the law, and
some just do not know any better, so it is impossible to imagine that human perfection is
likely to happen any time soon.
13810 Administration of Community Se ntences and Orders Bill 26 Sep 2013
New Zealand First supports the move to re move barriers in managing offenders in
the community in a manner that is safe, hu mane, secure, effective, and, of course,
efficient. It is important that  New Zealanders have confiden ce in our justice system and
that offenders are made accountable for th eir actions to the community they have
offended against. It is therefore crucial that the way we manage offenders in our
communities is done with no room for any mistakes or any errors. We all know the
consequences of mistakes. They leave communities worried about their safety,
something that we should not allow to happen.
We read in the news this week about a 19-year-old and his girlfriend who violated a
young 10-year-old girl. The Administration of  Community Sentencing and Orders Bill
must close the loopholes that could lead to this kind of immoral and unacceptable
behaviour in our community.
The Law and Order Committee report proposed  amendments that were intended to
improve the original bill. Those amendments are encouraging. Community-based
sentences were introduced in New Zealand fo r many reasons. It would be interesting to
see a report on any improvements made sin ce their introduction. They are to reduce
incarceration, relieve the overcrowding of prisons, offer a more appropriate sentence for
crimes of less gravity, and reduce costs to the Department of Corrections.
Why, then, two decades after non-custodial  sentences being introduced, have we
become a nation with too many people in our corrections system? Why is it that our
Government continues to look for more ideas for being productive in building more
prisons and enhancing the high incarceration statistics in New Zealand? Are people in
New Zealand committing more crime, or ar e people just enjoying being involved in
criminal activities? It is time for us to look at other techniques to prevent crime.
Whether this bill is the answer is, I think, a crucial question.
This bill seeks to ensure we do not trap people in a web where they constantly come
in and out of prison, wasting their lives and adding more burden to the taxpayers. New
Zealand First knows that the provision allo wing community magist rates to alter or
cancel a community-based sentence previously imposed by a community magistrate
means that this will allow the Chief Execu tive of the Department of Corrections to
approve changes of address for home or comm unity detention. Hopefully it will not be
the same mess created in the “Beast of Blenheim” case. Although New Zealand First
recognises the valid intention behind this approach, I would like to mention here the
need for accountability to be maintained. Sh ifting administrative responsibility should
not create cover-ups or loopholes in terms of accountability.
This bill has also been amended to allow a probation officer, rather than the court, to
direct that up to 20 percent of a community  work sentence of at least 80 hours be spent
in training. This is a good in itiative. This is a good way forward. As a strong advocate
of rehabilitation and reintegration, I cannot emphasise more the need for the probation
service and the Department of Corrections to work together to manage community-
based sentences. This bill, in general, will give probation officers more powers in
directing a proportion of community work sent ences into training. Reducing barriers to
enable training for offenders should be encouraged.
And yes, offenders need training, but New Zeal and First asks what the cost is to the
taxpayer. How many offenders with community  work sentences actually need training?
This information is important and would neces sitate funding for re levant resources as
well. From previous reports there were conc erns that with the increased imposition of
community service there is evidence that t hose sentenced to it are more likely to be
those who would otherwise have received fines but could not afford them.
It will be crucial that  probation officers use thes e new proposed powers with
discretion. No doubt there will be conflicting ideas and differences of opinion between
26 Sep 2013 Administration of Commun ity Sentences and Orders Bill 13811
what the judiciary and proba tion officers may recommend. In terms of the sentencing
hierarchy, we are making a change here thro ugh this bill, giving what were once the
powers of the judge to the probation officers. Guess what that means? I believe it means
that the Minister of Corrections has comp lete confidence in the probation service to
perform these vital roles for New Zealanders. Does she have that? I would like to hear a
response from the Minister, or for her to take a call and answer this question. What
evidence does she have to confirm her confidence?
It is interesting to see the recommendation that a court may not cancel or replace the
first sentence if that sentence was imposed by a higher court, but may instead remit the
matter to the court that imposed the first sent ence. Let us just hope that the higher court
will always get it right. Consistency in our judicial system is important and the
administration of community sentencing orde rs must always be aligned across all
Government departments. If something is to be implemented, it should be done to the
best of one’s ability to achieve the maximum quality results.
To do so, however, one needs the right tools to do the job. The probation service will
need to be sufficiently resourced to ensure that mandatory pre-sentence reports are done
to the correct and highest standard. This wi ll also ensure that when offenders are
directed to training, the probation service has the time to organise the best, appropriate
programmes for offenders—not just someone w ho comes off the road and says “I can
do this. I can deliver it. Just  because I can talk to the prisoner, I have the best
programme to ensure that this  person does not offend again.”  In recent years there have
been a lot of cases where placements in programmes for various offenders have been
poorly assessed.
A probation officer can now review the suitability of the home detention residence or
curfew address. This is when the court de fers the commencement of a second sentence
of home or community detention for more than 2 months and indicates that for the
purpose of determining when post-detention conditions commence, any concurrent or
cumulative home detention sentences will be treated as a notional single sentence.
The other part of the proposed amendments includes where an appeal against a home
detention sentence is unsuccessful. There is a requirement for the registrar of the appeal
court to notify the controlling officer of the relevant probation area, and the offender, if
they are not in court, of the date on which the sentence resumes.
So community safety is vital and absolute ly a priority for our nation. New Zealand
First strongly believes that to achieve eff ective law and order in our nation, the public
should have confidence in our judiciary, our  police, and the corrections system. I
believe we can all accept the fact that for a nation of our  size we have far too many
people in our corrections system. Let me once again remind the National Government
that a genuine Government is not a searcher for consensus but a moulder of consensus.
New Zealand First supports the initiative to fix up the loopholes, and supports what this
bill intends to do.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to rise and speak in the
Committee stage of the Administration of Community Sentences and Orders Bill.
Labour is obviously supporting this bill. As has already been said, the bill makes a
number of technical amendments, predominat ely to Acts, and a few policy changes that
Phil Goff, who was the Minister at the time, I believe, presided over—the Parole Act, in
particular, and the Sentencing Act in its original form.
Before I get into the detail of the bill, I do want to make some general statements
about the justice area as it relates to community-based sentencing in particular. We have
had Ministers from that side  of the House trumpet for some time now that there has
been a decrease in reported  crimes, that the National Government’s “tough on crime”
stance has been the cause of this reducti on and its much-heralded success. The honest
13812 Administration of Community Se ntences and Orders Bill 26 Sep 2013
truth is that, actually, globally, there have been drops in recorded crime. There has been
much interesting debate as to why this gl obal trend has occurred, and there have been
some very interesting theories, but ther e seems to be consensus that it does not
necessarily come down to the domestic pol icies of a Government. So that is an
interesting contextual point to make.
We do hear constantly in our domestic politics about this “tough on crime” line, both
by the National Party when it was in Opposition and as an ongoing sentiment when in
Government. But what changes when National comes into Government is the way it is
executed—“tough on crime” in rhetoric, but su ddenly it is OK with things like home
detention, which we are debating today. At the time, as I recall, when Labour trumpeted
the need for these kinds of sentences and for community-based sentences, there were
some Government members who were veheme ntly opposed to any ex ploration of those
kinds of sentences. So it seems extraordinary to me that the Government maintains this
rhetoric whilst actually ac knowledging that what Labour has always been is smart on
crime. We do what works. We listen to the evidence and the research, and we invest
where it is necessary. We are willing to be bold and courage ous and to invest in areas
like community-based sentencing because not only, as Bill English has said, it is a fiscal
imperative because the justice sector is costing us so mu ch but also you see reduced
rates of reoffending when you use methodology like this.
Surely the focus should be on how you balance the need for someone who commits a
crime to pay their debt to society with ensu ring that we make the community safer by
ensuring that we actually change something fo r that person’s life, both in the way that
they are reintegrated into society and also in the way they are rehabilitated. There are
flaws—I know the Minister of Corrections  knows this. I know she knows it because
quietly behind the scenes  she is doing things a little bi t differently, but not letting it
undermine her “tough on crime” sentiment. She k nows that ultimately things have to be
done differently if we are to make any ga ins in this area. Even Bill English has
stipulated that.
I also want to highlight, as I have sa id, home detention. From 2007-08 and 2008-09,
the offenders who were sentenced to hom e detention in that  period who were
reconvicted in the next 12 months sat at around 21 percent and 23 percent, respectively.
That was less than half the number of those released from a short-term prison sentence
in the same years, where reoffending rates sat at around more like 50 percent. So not
only do you see a significant saving for th e taxpayer and not onl y do you see those
offenders pay their debt to society by the cons traint on their liberty, albeit in a different
form than a formal imprisonment, but we actually see that the success rate attached to
that is much, much better. So there are many reasons why the strategic use of these
community-based sentences and things like home detention should be encouraged and
used appropriately.
In the face of that kind of evidence, we  still see a National Government that is
inclined to talk about the corrections syst em moving more towards a privatised model.
