We saw this U-turn, this claim that it was not going to turn existing public prisons into
private prisons, and it was going to do it only to new builds. But then it did it anyway
with the Serco contract at Mt Eden prison. That  actually sits in direct conflict with what
the Minister has been trying to do on the rehabilitation side of things within the
corrections portfolio. She may claim that gr oups like Serco have an interest in these
areas and can deliver the kind of rehabilitati on in the corrections system that she is
driving for, but the Minister knows that as soon as you drop down in your staffing
ratios, the less time that you have with prisoners  out of their cells, and the less time that
is available for you to offer those programmes, it upsets the entire system. The Minister
knows that because she also knows that those are the kinds of arguments that are made
26 Sep 2013 Administration of Commun ity Sentences and Orders Bill 13813
by prison officers all the time. Properly staffing prisons is a key part of ensuring that we
can deliver those much-needed programmes, so that we do not waste time and send
someone back into the circle of reoffending. They are inextr icably linked with proper
staffing and proper support of staffing in corr ections facilities, and that is something
that I have no doubt we will continue to ra ise with this Minister—the very unsafe
environments, which I know exist and which corrections officers are exposed to.
Coming back to the bill, I mentioned that there are some substantive policy changes
but then also some more technical ones. I ha d a couple of questions for the Minister on
some of those. I know she will excuse the fact that I was not part of the select
committee process. One of the changes to th e Sentencing Act in particular allows pre-
sentence reports for home detention or comm unity detention. Offenders are sometimes
sentenced to home detention, and that requires  an assessment of home circumstances to
ensure suitability. There are some changes there also on, I think, post-release, where the
writing of those reports are handed over fr om the probation service to the chief
executive. I just wondered about capacity, to  ensure that that handover can be managed
properly and ensure that it is happening in a timely fashion. There are also changes that
have been made to when home detention is  cancelled when a subsequent sentence of
imprisonment is applied. A court cannot order that an ex isting home detention sentence
resumes once someone leaves prison. That is just a common-sense change. Again, it
demonstrates why Labour is in support of these amendments.
Also there is an alignment of electroni c monitoring conditions with the range of
monitoring equipment. That was something th at Kris Faafoi touched on, and I will not
traverse that again, but it did make me w onder, Minister, whether or not there were
elements where it related to the developing technology, and whether or not there was a
way that that did not need to be included in  primary legislation, given that there might
be ongoing amendments of a technical nature th at relate to the technology as it updates.
That would prevent us from having to come back to the House with primary legislation
to ensure that issues like this are dealt w ith. I do not know whether or not that was ever
feasible, but it was a question that I thought I would raise. But in that change, it says
that offenders may go beyond the boundaries  of electronic monitoring equipment
without breaching their conditi ons because although they may stray from the electronic
boundary, they must remain within the resi dence boundary. This makes it difficult to
successfully prosecute.
Alongside that, in one of the technical am endments, is the requirement to tell or
inform someone with a home detention se ntence of the boundary that they have
applying to them, and to tell it to those who live on the property of the boundary that
applies to the prisoner, as well. I wondered whether or not  there had been cases where
you had been able to prosecute, Minister, because it was found that they were not
properly informed. Is that one of the reasons now to close that loophole that is in the
legislation? I wondered whether there had been any cases where the combination of
those two issues had led to unsuccessful prosecutions around breaches of conditions. It
was just something I was interested in. Also, it seems common sense that if someone
has a boundary applied to them for home dete ntion, they would be told about it, but I
guess there have been circumstances where th at has not happened, given that it is now
going to be clarified in the legislation.
There is a question here as well around ensu ring the integrity of the sentences. Time
continues to run on a co mmunity-based sentence after an application to vary or cancel
this sentence is made. So that means, I be lieve, that if there is non-compliance, the
sentence can actually be put on hold until there is a variation, and then it resumes. What
kind of time period—I am not sure; the La w and Order Committee members may have
discussed this—may apply for that variation?  I would be interested to know how long
13814 Administration of Community Se ntences and Orders Bill 26 Sep 2013
that is suspended for. I am assuming that, of course, they still required to comply, but
the sentence itself is suspended. So they stil l have to be compliant during the variation,
but they then have to technically fulfil the sentence afterwards . That would be my
understanding, but I would be interested to ha ve the Minister correct me if I am wrong
in that sense.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I rise to make so me comments on the
Administration of Community Sentences and Or ders Bill. I begin by saying that we all
acknowledge—in fact, the Government spends a lot of time telling us—that we have a
lower crime rate, although I think that the reality is we have an increasingly lower
prosecution rate. We know that police officers and the police force have been instructed
to minimise the number of charges that they now lay against offenders, and that
therefore reduces the prosecution rate. It makes the figures look good, but there is a real
question about whether the crime rate is actually dropping.
That said, once we get to the offenders themselves, and certa inly the convicted
offenders, policies that are focused on both correction and rehabilitation are much better
than those that are focused just on th e more punitive elements that go with
incarceration. So that is why, as a general principle, we in Labour are supportive of this
bill, of this legislation, and, indeed—as I th ink Kris Faafoi acknowledged, credit where
credit is due—of some of the measures th at the present Minister  of Corrections has
taken to assist those who are presently incarcera ted to make a real fist of adjusting post-
release. We know that ther e are good programmes in the prisons now on literacy, on
work readiness, and on community readiness, if you like—getting ready to go back into
the community. I was greatly privileged in the visit that I, Kris Faafoi, and Darien
Fenton took to P āremoremo prison earlier this year to see one of the programmes in
place and the efforts that had been taken to have people adjust, ready for post-release.
But it is better if we can avoid incarceration—acknowledging that there needs to be a
punishment and acknowledging that there needs to be sanction. Where it is at all
possible for sentences to be served in the community—whether through home
detention, through a curfew, or through othe r community sentences —that is surely
better. And just as we can say with some cer tainty that there are some people for whom
prison is inevitable because of the nature of  their offending, their violent personality, or
their antisocial personality, equally we can say that there are some people for whom
prison is completely the wrong thing. Th ey may act antisocially, they may be
committing crimes—certainly at the low end of the scale—and generally they will be
younger people. They are the ones whom, if we  possibly can avoid it, we should avoid
sending to prison. So a community-based sentence is entirely appropriate.
We welcome this legislation, which tidies up some of those aspect s and that enables
the courts to deal with community sentences that need to be extended or adjusted or
amended. There is now a process for doing th at. That gives proba tion officers, whose
role is to get close to offenders in the co mmunity and manage their rehabilitation in the
community, greater scope to assist the offenders for whom they are responsible to adjust
and to adapt. That, hopefully—we are optimistic, and we should be confident—will lead
to a lower recidivism rate and a more e ffective process for re habilitation. So we
welcome all those aspects of it.
We should not forget that people with community sentences, pa rticularly curfews
and home detention, and, indeed, those peopl e who are required to provide work and
contribute their efforts for a certain period of  hours, still have a restriction on liberty.
There are plenty of people in the community  who forget that it is the restriction on
liberty that is the ultimate punishment for people whom, when they offend against our
criminal statutes, we call for sanctions upon. It is that restriction of  liberty th at is the
sanction. But we need to make sure that having done that in this sort of way, the
26 Sep 2013 Administration of Commun ity Sentences and Orders Bill 13815
mechanisms and the tools that we have to ma nage those sorts of sentences are effective
and offer sufficient flexibility.
We know with electronic monitoring that there has been a problem, and I know that
the regime or the governance of our electroni c monitoring in the criminal justice system
has been changed so that the Department of  Corrections now has a responsibility for it.
That is right. We have had people who have not only breached their electronic
monitoring conditions but absconded while  on home detention. We have had the
dreadful and unfortunate situation of the offender in Palmerston North who was on
home detention and being electronically monitored, who managed to get away—not just
get out of Palmerston North but get out of the country. He went to Canada and ended up
murdering a person there earlier this year. So it is good that we are beefing that up.
In terms of Part 2, the new arrangements , or the flexible ar rangements for amending
and changing sentences, make absolute sense. And in terms of new section 66A inserted
by clause 18A, I will acknowledge that I think that is a good change to allow some of
that community service, when it is for 80 hour s or more, to be regarded as training. I
acknowledge that and congratulat e the Minister on what I th ink will be a very good
move. It will allow those who have to do wo rk by way of penance for their offending to
actually get something out of it beyond just work experience. They will get something
that they can show for it—certification of what  they have done and their skills. I think
that will make a big difference to the sort s of people who find themselves as candidates
for this sort of sentencing.
I want to simply add a word of caution abou t one aspect of it. I know that this has
been through the Law and Order Committee,  and my colleagues on the committee and,
indeed, the Labour caucus have  supported it, but I do want to just make a note of
caution, really, with my pedantic, overzeal ous justice hat on—becau se you cannot be a
justice spokesperson without being a zealot , on occasions—in relation to new section
69JA inserted by clause 22A and new section 80FA inserted by clau se 27A, and that is
about the role of the chief executive. We kno w that the way this operates is, of course,
that it is not the chief executiv e. It will not be Ray Smith sitting in his office, approving
all these changes of residence and locations for the way these sentences are going to be
served out; it is going to be somebody in th e Department of Corr ections who will have
this responsibility.
My concern is that these sentences are im posed by judges, by officers of the court.
They carry a judicial imprimatur and a prope r judicial sanction. There is oversight by
the probation service—that is kind of the opera tional end of the criminal justice system.
I understand all that, but I get a little nervous when  it comes to adjusting and changing
what are, effectively, orders of the court. They go to an official, the identity of whom
may well be unknown, and therefore the account ability for that may be somewhat
diffuse. I simply raise that point and get it on the record so that in the unfortunate event,
and, hopefully, unlikely event, that somethi ng does go wrong with this administration,
that has been noted. I am sure that a consci entious Minister of Corrections, for as long
as she is in the role, at least, would at so me point want to review the practices that
emerge around all this and the track record and, if it calls for it and if there are too many
unfortunate events, want to maybe look at whet her it is appropriate for a senior official
within the Department of Corrections to  be making or mandating these changes or
whether or not it should go back to the cour t—even the registrar of the court—or at
least to have some expedited process within th e court, to ensure that the decisions that
get taken with regard to the offender who is being managed at all times have the
imprimatur of a judge in terms of the sentence the offender is serving and carrying out.
Notwithstanding all that, as my colleagues have said, we support the legislation. It
does have the potential to offer some good and effective changes and a more positive
13816 Administration of Community Se ntences and Orders Bill 26 Sep 2013
future for those offenders who find themselves in this situation but who can be managed
in the community, can serve out their time and suffer the sanction that is imposed on
them, and turn out to be good citizens at  the end of that. That is a welcome
development.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I am pleased to take a brief ca ll on behalf of the Green Party
in support of this legislation, the Administ ration of Community Sentences and Orders
Bill. I hope the Minister of Corrections  is coping with the Greens supporting two
initiatives in 1 week. It is possibly groundbreaking. I do want to offer formally in this
Chamber congratulations on the change in th e policy around transgender prisoners. It
will make a huge difference to people’s lives, and that is a wonderful thing.
We are supporting this legislation. It is abso lutely consistent with our view in terms
of justice and the best evidence of what works in this country. We recognise that
primarily it is made up around administrative changes to make the system more efficient
in relation to community sentences and orde rs in the community, but there are some
minor drafting amendments that are significant  in terms of policy, and we also support
those.
The drafting amendments are primarily to the Sentencing Act, the Parole Act, and the
Bail Act. The minor policy changes will improve the effectiveness and efficiency of
home detention, community-based sentences,  and the electronic monitoring regime.
That relates mostly, it seems, from my read ing of the bill, to now matching when an
offender is released into the community with  electronic monitoring, to ensure that they
are living in an area that is  capable of being monitored by that electronic monitoring
system. That just seems an incredibly logical thing to match. It does not really seem
very sensible that people are being released into areas that cannot be monitored in this
system, and apparently there are some occasions where offenders have been on
community sentences and they have been  bunking out on them and, on occasion, have
not been found until the end of that sentence.
I guess the core of our system working is th at people take responsibility and they are
held accountable for their actions. Clearly, that  was not the case with the system in that
situation. So an amendment to ensure that there is the abi lity for an application to be
made to vary or cancel the sentence to matc h that and to ensure that they are held
accountable does seem to be appropriate and consistent with the intent of the legislation.
We also support the move to focus more on rehabilitation. Clearly that is something
that works for all of us. Enabling probati on officers to direct up to 20 percent of
sentences to be spent in working and living skills courses without the need to apply to
the court is also a really positive measure. We all know that sometimes education can
make a difference as well as those wraparound services that people have talked about.
We certainly would like to see more investment in those because we believe that they
really work, and the evidence shows us that. To streamline that system, to enable people
to get access to those things, is just a sensible and good thing.
This bill is around improving that system of  community-based sentences. It has been
mentioned earlier, but it is worth restating that we know that the recidivism rate is much
lower with community-based sentences. Clearl y, part of that is going to be because
there is a threshold in terms of the seri ousness of a crime a nd the likelihood of
somebody being caught up in criminality that would be more likely in a prison
environment, but it is also because of the nature of the sentencing. There is something
about the limitation of somebody remaining in their community that can hold them into
more positive outcomes at times. This is something that potentially saves us money in
that financial bottom line. It is a good social result and a good economic result.
We would like to encourage more of thos e kinds of solutions, so we are supporting
this bill.
26 Sep 2013 Administration of Commun ity Sentences and Orders Bill 13817

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I am happy to take a brief call on the
Administration of Community Sentences and Orders Bill.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: So are we.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: My colleague Clayton Cosgrove is very excited about the fact
that I am speaking on this bill. I want to  just begin by placing a caution around the use
of official crime statistics, because, in my view, 99 percent of official crime statistics
are rubbish because they are very easily ma nipulated. They are based on reported crime
normally, and there are a whole lot of factors that impact on whether,  in fact, the crime
is reported in the first place. I am getting some very interesting looks from Mr Sabin
over there, but official crime statistics are very easily manipulated.
In fact, if we look at them over time—whic h is often where we use crime statistics;
we look at them over time—actually, societ al norms around what  is reported often
changes. If you look at official crime statisti cs for domestic violence, for example, the
reporting of domestic violence is now mo re common than it used to be. A lot of
domestic violence previously went unreported, but there are a whole lot of reasons why
a lot of the domestic violence that takes place today still goes unreported. So the official
crime statistics can often be incredibly misleading, and I th ink we need to be a little
cautious—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: You can’t report what you don’t know about.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I know about it. I know quite a lot about it, ac tually. And we
need—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: No, no—I say people can’t report what they don’t know about.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Yes, that’s right. People ca nnot report—absolutely. But that
simply reinforces the point that the official  crime statistics can be misleading and that
we need to be very careful about placing a lot of emphasis on official crime statistics
when we are making decisions.
I do want to, however, compliment the Gove rnment for this piece of legislation
actually, because this is the sort of legisla tion that the National Party would have likely
railed against when it was in Opposition. In fact, it did rail against many of the very
measures that are in this bill  and that it was vehemently opposed to when it was last in
Opposition. I am pleased to see that it has seen  the light and in fact  it is now willing to
make decisions in this area ba sed on what actually works. If we want to get serious
about reducing recidivism and reducing reo ffending, we do actually need to look at the
evidence of what works, rather than looking  at what is going to  be popular, because
those two things are quite often very diffe rent. No Government and no Opposition ever
won votes by promising to be soft on crime, and no Government or Opposition ever lost
votes through the reverse. It is very clear that there is definitely a public appetite for
Governments and for political parties to be hard on crime. There is a clear public
appetite for that. But, actually, things lik e many of the measures contained in this
legislation actually—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: I think it’s being effective on crime.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Effective on crime? That is quite right, actually—we do need—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Effective policing, effective on crime.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Telling cops to lay fewer charges is not being effective on crime.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Well, actually, Mike Sabin makes a very good point—it is about
being effective on crime. But Andrew Little also makes an even better point, which is
that telling cops to under-report crime does not actually make us more effective on
crime at all. Unfortunately, there is enough of that going on at the moment where crimes
are going unreported and they are not being recorded in the official crime statistics. That
does not mean that they are not happening; it just means that they are not being
adequately reported. I think that is fundamentally wrong.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. Thank you very much
for this opportunity to contribute in this Committee stage debate on the Administration
of Community Sentences and Orders Bill. It is a shame that my colleague Jan Logie,
unfortunately, cannot also reap some of the prai se that I want to give to the Minister of
Corrections. I want to acknowledge the announcement yesterday in terms of transgender
and transsexual prisoners. I think it is not  a bold move but a move that she has made
based on the evidence and also based on the work of people like Jan Logie to advocate
for our transgender community.
My contribution to this debate is really to highlight again the contribution that our
probation officers give to the whole smooth r unning of the justice system. Actually, if
there was one thing that I really wanted to highlight, it is that this piece of legislation
now empowers them with more  responsibility and with more opportunity to do their
job, which is, to quote from their website, to “protect the public and help reduce re-
offending by supporting offenders by bringing about positive changes.” So I see that the
opportunity that this piece of legislation gives to them will actually enable more robust
relationships with community organisations.
One of the things that I have seen in my electorate of Manurewa and the probation
service that we provide is that a lot of the community work that the service tries to find
is actually about reintegrating and enabling some of our offenders  whom, for whatever
reason—drunk-driving, family violence issues—w e want to reintegrate. Some of the
specific connections that we were trying to encourage in my electorate were work in
schools, for example, and work supporting not only sports organisations but also some
of our social sector organisations. The overall theme and strategy about enabling people
to contribute and feel like they are part of the community is, I think, completely
underlined in this piece of legislation. I do want to congratulate the Government on
what it is doing.
We have some challenges in the jus tice system. Too many  of our young people—
and, actually, older people—are doing things , particularly around alcohol, drugs, and
public behaviour, which mean that one of the mechanisms we have is to sentence them
to home detention or community detention. The overall strategy and philosophy that this
26 Sep 2013 Administration of Commun ity Sentences and Orders Bill 13819
piece of legislation is bringing in is real ly about giving people second chances and
enabling them to feel like they do have a pathway to a better life and a better
contribution.
I particularly want to focus, I guess, on the translation of some of the community
work to people being able to do courses. I th ink it is a really constructive thing for the
justice system to encourage, so I am particularly encouraged by this general philosophy.
It seems that there is a consensus right th rough the Committee in terms of this kind of
justice engagement. We want people to get th e support and help that they need so that
they do not stay there for life. I think that is one of the biggest challenges when I look at
who is in prison. Because of the Wiri Pris on being developed in my community, I have
a relationship with Serco. I have been to Mt  Eden prison. I know that this type of
philosophy we can start at this lower offe nding end of the spectrum, but it actually
needs to permeate right through our criminal justice system. In terms of this philosophy,
I am really encouraged.
I again want to congratulat e the Minister of Correcti ons and also the people who
worked on this bill. I am not on the Law and Order Committee, but I acknowledge those
members of the House who are. I do see this as another constructive opportunity for us
to work together. I think a ll of us do not want people in  prisons. We want to stop
building prisons. We actually want to make sure that people who do enter the justice
system at this end—the beginning end, I gue ss—of what could be a pathway for them
being in the justice system for life actua lly have a pathway out. That is why I
particularly stand in support of this bill and commend this bill to the Committee.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I move, That the Insolvency
Practitioners Bill be  now read a second time . Insolvency practitioners carry out a
number of different insolvency proce sses, including liqui dations, voluntary
administrations, and receiverships. These pr ocesses require a practitioner to carry out
skilled tasks with sound judgment and integr ity in order to protect and promote an
efficient and effective corporate insolvency system. There is general consensus amongst
reputable insolvency practitioners that there is a small number of practitioners who are
continually underperforming and imposing si gnificant costs upon cr editors and failing
to discharge their statutory obligations. These problems revolve around competency,
unethical behaviour, and insufficient monitoring.
The Insolvency Practitioners Bill wa s drafted in 2008 under the previous
Government to create a negative licensing regi me to regulate insolvency practitioners.
Negative licensing would enable  any person to prac tise as an insolvency practitioner
unless they were prohibited. It was seen as a low-cost, light-handed regulatory approach
to strengthen an enforcement void: the abil ity to remove incompetent and dishonest
insolvency practitioners from the market.
The Commerce Committee considered the bill at  the end of 2010 and in the first part
of 2011. I would like to thank the committee for the constructive time spent undertaking
a thorough examination of the bill. The bill received 11 submissions and most
submitters did not think the bill went far enough to address the problems in the
insolvency market. Submitters argued that in  the intervening time, the global financial
crisis had meant that there was an increase in insolvency work and an increase in the
number of insolvency practitioners taking a ppointments. This meant that the magnitude
of the problems had become more evident. The select committee carefully considered
options for regulating insolvency practitioners and reported back to the House on 9 May
2011 its recommendation to adopt a registratio n model, instead of a negative licensing
regime.
Under the bill as reported back, all insolv ency practitioners will now be required to
be registered in order to accept insolvency appointments. The Registrar of Companies
will have enhanced oversight and enforcem ent mechanisms, including the power to
deregister substandard or delinquent individuals. I suppor t this recommendation. It is
important that corporate insolvencies are car ried out professionally and efficiently. This
bill is part of the Government’s focus on improving the integrity of our financial
systems. It is important that we boost inve stor confidence and that investors have the
confidence in our markets. It is especially important that investors know that if an
insolvency practitioner is goi ng to look into the affairs of a company, they can have
confidence that it can be done and will be done with integr ity, and that the insolvency
practitioner has the minimum skills for the job.
A register held by the company’s office will give the public access to basic and
standardised information about practitioners  who are registered. Through the register,
the Registrar of Companies will be able to collect information and regulate practitioners
more effectively. The bill is set to come into force 9 months after the date on which it
26 Sep 2013 Insolvency Practitioners Bill 13821
receives the Royal assent. Insolvency practitioners have up to 3 months after this to
register. The operation of the registration regi me will be reviewed no later than 4 years
after the legislation comes into force to r ecommend whether any further amendments to
the regime would be necessary or desirable. More specifically, the bill as reported back
will amend the Companies Act 1993 and the Receiverships Act 1993 to make clear how
the appointment of insolvency practitione rs to, and the removal of insolvency
practitioners from, the register will work. There will be new provisions, including the
eligibility criteria, enhanced duties, and criteria for disqualification, and an appropriate
range of penalties for failure to comply with statutory obligations. Under the
amendments, a person can apply for a court order to override any removal from the
register.
One important amendment is greater transparency so that creditors must be provided
with relevant information by insolvency prac titioners at the earliest opportunity. This
includes a statement of interest by the insolvency practitioner and an additional report to
the registrar that summarises the insolvency. This new regime will be a significant
improvement and will help with the rec ognition and detection of incompetent and
unethical persons, who will either be prevented from registering or have their
registration cancelled.
A substantial amount of work has been goi ng on behind the scenes since the bill was
reported back from the select committee. I am pleased that this bill is now continuing its
progression through the House. At th e appropriate time I will introduce a
Supplementary Order Paper that proposes further amendments to the bill to better align
requirements for the different types of pract itioners and clarify the obligations of
practitioners. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: It is an interesting fact that the number
of insolvencies since 2008 has increased dramatically under this Government. One
could probably point, without getting off the mark too much, to many in the export
sector who, because of the high dollar and th e lack of any sort of initiative over
monetary policy, have been forced to the wa ll, not because of their own negligence, but
because of the environment they face and th e lack of a supportive Government to stand
alongside them.
However, putting that aside, we support this bill, the Insolvency Practitioners Bill.
But it is also interesting to note the gestation period for this  piece of legislation, which
had its genesis way back in a 2004 Ministry  of Economic Development report that was
produced under the last Government. That report raised some serious concerns in
respect of a minority of pr actitioners who, it was allege d, were—bluntly—incompetent
or lacked the skills that were required to carry out insolvency work. There were
submitters to the report who talked about di shonesty, negligence, and an inability to
carry out the principal duties that were required.
If you look at the history, it is also inte resting to note that the existing criteria
basically say if you are over 18, breathing, wa lking upright, and without any particular
educational or tertiary qualifications or skills in the area, it is possible for you to engage
in insolvency work. That is a deficiency. I have got to say that  if you look at the
legislative history of this—t he bill was introduced unde r, I think, the Minister’s
predecessor Simon Power. He nods—indeed. He was a good Minister. He used to chug
things through. It is a pity  he is not here, because it has slowed down somewhat now.
The bill was introduced on 27 April 2010, ha d its first reading on 21 August 2010, and
went before the Commerce Committee on 9 May 2011—and, hey presto, here we are, a
few years later, and suddenly this bill has b ecome a high priority. Maybe the Minister is
trying to fill up his day—I do not know. Maybe the diary is a bit light—I am not sure—
13822 Insolvency Practitioners Bill 26 Sep 2013
but this is an important piece of legislation that should indeed have been given a higher
degree of priority.
We support this bill because it builds on a variety of, if you like, consumer protection
legislation, but it also builds in protections for those credito rs who are on the receiving
end of insolvencies. One that comes to mind,  I have got to say, is the collapse of
Mainzeal Property and Construction, wher e many, many people lost their jobs. Many
subcontractors, for instance, were caught in a situation where they  could not get their
tools of trade. They could not move on. They were not the negligent parties. They could
not move on and get into other jobs and ge t other income. They were caught between a
rock and a hard place. That was a high-profile collapse.
I do note, just in passing, for the recor d, that the Rt Hon Dame Jenny Shipley was a
key director of that company and also, I think, a key direct or of Genesis Energy, one of
our State-owned enterprises. To date we  have had no explanation—no explanation—as
to why that collapse happened, who was imp licated, and who was responsible. It even
came before—I see Mr Young, the chair of the Commerce Committee, here—the
Commerce Committee, almost a year ago to the day. Given that Mrs Shipley heads up
one of our State-owned enterprises, we tried to pose some questions—because it goes to
the credibility and integrity of other work  that she may do for the Crown—and to ask
what the problem was. I think her comment was “I will not offend the Standing Orders
by answering that question.”, or words to that ef fect. So it is interesting that for those in
lofty places—those who have been in seni or positions in Government, who know the
rules, and who are now in the private sector—suddenly there is a lack of accountability.
It does not flow straight through.
We support the legislation. We believe this is  appropriate legislation. I know that Mr
Young, as chair of the Commerce Committee, is desperate to get up and talk about it. It
is necessary. I am reminded of a story in resp ect of the head of Tait Electronics, the late
Sir Angus Tait. He said at a speech I was at  many years ago that one of the greatest
learning periods—and I am characterising what he said—in his life in terms of business
was when that business almost hit the wa ll and he had the receiver looking over his
shoulder, and that great man managed to get the business back into being the wonderful
enterprise it is. But he made the point that he  learnt so much during that stressful period
about business.
This bill is about protecting creditors. This is also about ensuring that people who
have to manage and action insolvencies are actually qualified, are robust, and are people
of good character and not sharks. So it would be unusual if any part y in this House did
not support the legislation, but I say in conclusion that it has taken a long time—a long
time—for this Government to give it some pr iority. It should have had a higher priority
than it has at the present time, and I hope that the Minister will act with a higher degree
of efficiency when it comes to other, just as important legislation.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am pleased to stand in
support of the Insolvency Pract itioners Bill in its second reading. It came before the
Commerce Committee on 24 August 2010. During that time we received and considered
11 submissions from interested groups an d individuals, and we heard only one
submission from that period of time. So, essentially, it is not a large sector, but it is very
important, as the previous speaker, the Hon Clayton Cosgrove, said. When it comes to a
company that has gone into di fficulty and insolvency, it is  very import ant that the
person who oversees that has not only the ski lls but the credibility, because there are
lots of people—creditors, obviously—who ar e dependent upon the good work of that
person to recover as much as possible. We  know that it is important for our economy
that when things do go AWOL, when things do turn upside down, th at we can recover
as much as possible. We live in a very in terconnected economy, obviously, and so this
26 Sep 2013 Insolvency Practitioners Bill 13823
bill, in particular, is ensuring that we do have some very robust measures around those
people who are appointed as insolvency practitioners.
This bill is actually part of the Nationa l-led Government’s focus on improving the
integrity of our financial system. The pr evious speaker, the Hon Clayton Cosgrove,
talked about the number of companies th at have gone through difficulty since 2008. I
think that we need to be reminded again that the global financial crisis in 2008 and 2009
was the worst financial crisis  that has affected this ec onomy and the economies of the
world in over 60 years. Yes, it brought incredible stresses upon companies in New
Zealand for a variety of reasons. Obviously, during those times of pressure the system is
tested, and the integrity of our financial syst em in many regards stood up far, far better
than those in other jurisdictions around the world—our banking system, in particular.
The overriding focus of the commerce portfo lio is to restore the confidence of
investors and people who participate in our  economy and to bring confidence to our
capital markets, especially after the very, very difficult time when we saw so many
finance companies collapse. We are focused on boosting growth and creating jobs. Only
a strong economy can provide financial secu rity for families, real opportunities for
young people, safer communities, and the higher education and health services that all
New Zealanders need. This bill is a further measure in that process.
One of the things I want to talk about th rough that process that the committee looked
at is the appointment of family members. We considered clause 5 of the bill, as
introduced—

THURSDAY, 26 SEPTEMBER 2013 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
MOTIONS 
America’s Cup 2013—Emirates Team New Zealand 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Acting Prime Minister) : I seek leave to move without 
notice a motion in recognition of Team New Zealand’s efforts in the America’s Cup. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none.  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I move, That this House congratul ate Emirates Team New 
Zealand on its hard-fought campaign in the 2013 America’s Cup in San Francisco . 
Although the result was not what we were hoping for, we send congratulations to Oracle 
Team USA and admire their fighting spirit  and the ongoing improvements made to stay 
in the match and eventually take the c up. To Emirates Team New Zealand, you have 
made us proud, and we have loved every moment of watching your boat Aotearoa 
literally fly around San Francisco Bay. You caught the interest and attention of so many 
New Zealanders who did not expect to admire and become involved in the America’s 
Cup contest. You have competed hard on the water, and have conducted yourselves 
with dignity and professionalism off the wa ter. On behalf of 4.5 million Kiwis, 
congratulations on a great campaign. 
Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour) : I rise on behalf of the New 
Zealand Labour Party to s upport the motion. We congratulat e Oracle Team USA on a 
successful defence of the America’s Cup. It was a truly remarkable comeback. We send 
our commiserations to Grant Dalton, to Dean  Barker, and to the crew that made New 
Zealanders so proud. The sporting hopes of the nation were with Emirates Team New 
Zealand on every tack, every gybe, and every fo il. The crew did their very best, and it 
was a fantastic effort. We c ongratulate them. We record our admiration for the Kiwi 
ingenuity and innovation that saw New Z ealand boating and computer technology 
displayed to the world as the best in the world. That expertise, together with New 
Zealand’s extraordinary sailing excellence,  was just not quite enough on the day, and 
we, again, commiserate with Emirates Team New Zealand for gettin g so close but not 
quite winning.  
Can I pass on our admiration for how dignifi ed they have been in defeat. We should 
also be proud that in Oracle’s time of need they reached out to New Zealanders in order 
to get the extra boat speed that  they needed. This is truly an event that has brought New 
Zealanders together. As Grant Robertson said to me earlier, he understood that 
somewhere in a bar in San Francisco it ha s even brought Steven  Joyce and Trevor 
Mallard together singing Dave Dobbyn songs like “Loyal”. 
METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green): What a bugger, eh? What a race! We got 
this close; they got this close. New Zealan ders all over the worl d have been cheering 
Dean Barker, his team, and al l of the people who have work ed so hard to support this 
race. My message is do not worry, because New Zealanders are still behind you, Dean 
Barker, and all your team for all the amazing work you have done, no matter what the 
result. The catamarans are so closely matche d that there was some tantalising racing, 
with those flying catamarans travelling faster  than the speed of wind, and with lead 
changes, yachts on the edge of tipping over—what I heard one wit describe as “the cock 
of a dog’s leg”—and teams finishing within ju st seconds of each other. Race 10 of the 
final will no doubt be one of the greatest ya cht races of all time, but it was also a 
13770 Motions 26 Sep 2013 
turning-point race. Well done to Oracle Team USA. It really, truly was some comeback. 
To Team New Zealand—you did your country proud. Our hearts go out to you at this 
time of great agony over the result, having come so close.  
I suspect that technology was the winner  on the day for this cup—technology largely 
built by New Zealanders. We can be doubly pr oud that both boats were built mostly by 
New Zealanders here in New Zealand, and that Auckland is  now home to some of the 
most advanced boatbuilding t echniques in the wo rld. This America’s Cup will be good 
not only for our high-tech mari ne manufacturing industry but also for the thousands of 
bright New Zealanders whom it employs. Team New Zealand, you have provided us 
with a vision of a smart and green economy a nd a legacy that will not be lost, and there 
is, of course, always next time.  
Plus it is not all bad news on the sports  front today. Let us congratulate the New 
Zealand Football Ferns, which won the Va lais Cup in Switzerland this morning—a 
historic win for our women’s football t eam—and congratulations to New Zealand’s 
Amber Hearn, who was named player of the tournament. Thank you. 
RICHARD PROSSER (NZ First) : New Zealand First joins other parties in the 
House in congratulating Team New Zealand. The final result of the America’s Cup, 
even though a disappointment, when we came so close to winning, is  a time to reflect 
on what New Zealanders are capable of  achieving. Team New Zealand performed 
superbly against the scale and wealth of th e United States team, a team that had the 
resources and the money to be able to bring in whomever and whatever it wanted at the 
last minute, a team for whom money was no object. Olympic champions and advanced 
technology were available to  the United States team—jus t a phone call away, at the 
snap of the fingers, never mind the cost. And there is the irony that the winning boat 
was actually built in New Zealand. In that sense, New Zealand is a winner.  
Our boat builders have shown that they ha ve excellence in the world, just as our 
sailors have shown through regattas the wo rld over, in every winning international 
team, that they are also the best in the world. New Zealand First congratulates Team 
New Zealand on their performance in the Am erica’s Cup in San Francisco. We applaud 
Dean Barker, the crew, and all who contribu ted to this outstanding effort. We applaud 
the families and the friends of the crew, and the legion of fine, patriotic supporters who 
outlaid such time and effort, who stuc k by their team—our team—through thick and 
thin, through the good times and the bad, right to the bitter end, a nd who are still there 
for our boys.  
We applaud Team New Zealand for their sportsmanship. We applaud them for their 
grit and determination. We applaud their conduct as exemplary ambassadors for New 
Zealand. In their gracious and commendabl e second placing—a silver medal for the 
silver fern team—they have enhanced New Zealand’s reputation. The world sees us and 
them in the light of old-fashioned good sportsmanship and gentlemanly conduct, and 
that will serve us well going into the future and into the next 4 years, because, like 
everyone else, I am sure that Team New Zealand will be back for another crack the next 
time the auld mug is up for grabs.  
Whatever happens next time, New Zeala nd and New Zealanders will be at the 
forefront of the competition for yachting’s gr eatest prize—the prize that is rightfully 
ours and will be again. New Zealanders will build the next generation of America’s Cup 
boats, and New Zealanders will crew them . One day we will bring the cup home again. 
This is not a time for mourning. It is not a time for disappoi ntment. It is a time for all 
New Zealanders to say to our team “We ll done. Good on you. New Zealand is proud of 
you.” Thank you. 
TE URUROA FLAVELL (Co-Leader—M āori Party): Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker, kia 
ora tātou katoa. Hei whaiwhai haere i te āhuatanga o te kōrero a ngā kaikōrero i mua i a 
26 Sep 2013 Motions 13771 
au, ko t āku he tautoko i ng ā kōrero katoa. Me mihi r ā ki a r ātou, ki a Dean Barker, me 
tana kāhui, ki a Grant Dalton, r ātou katoa i angitu, i m āia ki te tū i te mura o te ahi, e ai 
ki ngā kōrero. Ko te pai o t ērā hunga i te ata nei k āre i tuohu te m āhunga, kāre i piko te 
tuarā, kāre i taka te ngutu o te waha, kāre i noho whakamuri ēngari i māia, i angitu, i aro 
nui ki te kaupapa i wh āia e r ātou i te ata nei ka mutu, i ng ā wiki e 3 kua hipa ake. Me 
mihi ki a r ātou ka tika m ō te āhuatanga o te t ū, he t ū tangata, he t ū tika, he t ū m ō te 
motu e noho mai nei i te w ā kāinga, otirā, kāore e kore ko ng ā mea o Aotearoa wh ānui 
tonu i te ao. 
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and greetings to us all. To follow on with the tenor of the 
sentiments by speakers before me, I endorse all the tributes accord ed. We must indeed 
express a tribute to them, Dean Barker, his crew, Grant Dalton, all of them who fought 
on and according to accounts were tenacious at the battle-front. What was wonderful 
about that group this morning was that the he ad did not cower, the back did not bend, 
and the lip did not drop. They did not hold back but were relentless, courageous, and 
remained focused on what they were trying to achieve this morning, and of course over 
the past 3 weeks. We must pay them a tribut e indeed for the stance they took for 
humanity, for the righteous, and for the ones of the nation that  remained here at home, 
and without a doubt for the ones from New Zealand worldwide.] 
 I join the words of congratulations to our team. They did us proud, and as I said, 
they did not step back, they did not drop th eir heads or their lips, they focused on the 
task right through to the end, and we can be  proud of them. I think you can learn a lot 
from studying some names. I had a quick Google of the word “oracle”, and apparently it 
means a person or thing regarded as an infallible authority. But if we look at Team New 
Zealand—and I suppose that is th e catch for all of us—every one of us finds a space in 
Team New Zealand. Ka mihi ki a rātou ka tika. 
[We must indeed pay a tribute to them.] 
The great thing about our nation, I suppose, is the connections that we have. At home 
we can be proud of people like Ben Malcolm and Warren Houston, whose art adorns the 
hull of Aotearoa of Team New Zealand. Also, I thi nk we can admire the graphics of 
Ngāti Kahungunu and Ng āpuhi designer Ian Taylor, who I think captured the world 
with those graphics, but most im portant, I think, is the tie-in. P ēnei i a au a M āori nei, 
ka kite atu i te hononga o te waka hourua me t ēnei waka—me k ī, e ai ki ng ā kōrero o 
aku tūpuna i whakawhiti mai i Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa i te waka hourua. I ngā rā tata kua 
hipa ake, ar ā, ko taua waka, ko taua āhua an ō r ā, he waka hourua, ā, me k ī koina te 
kotahitanga o te whakaaro ao Māori, ao Pākehā. Ko ētahi ka kī, kāre he wāhanga o te ao 
Māori ki roto i t ēnei o ng ā kaupapa. Ko t āku, ko te k ī atu, ē, kai roto i taku DNA t ērā 
āhuatanga, mai i ōku tūpuna, i ōku mātua. Nō reira, koinei au e whai w āhi i roto i t ēnei 
o ng ā kaupapa ahakoa, ko te waka-ama, ko te waka hourua r ānei, he waka tonu, ā, 
koinei te āhuatanga o ōku tūpuna. 
[Like me as a M āori, I can see the connection of the double-hulled canoe with this 
vessel—that is to say, according to my an cestors they traversed the Pacific Ocean in a 
double-hulled canoe. In days just past we ha ve that similar vessel type doing the same 
thing. Let us suggest that it is the merging of M āori and non-M āori minds together as 
one. Some might say that M āoridom has no part to play in this of the ventures. But I 
would respond by saying steady on, that aspect  from my ancestors and parents is in my 
DNA. It is for this reason, therefore, that I am able to participate in this of the ventures, 
be it an outrigger vessel or a double-hulled one, it is st ill a canoe. As  far as my 
ancestors are concerned, this situation is still there.] 
I think we can be proud to fo cus not just on th e yacht race but on the presentation of 
ourselves as a nation. I want to acknowledge the efforts of Ng āti Whātua Ōrākei and Te 
Puni Kōkiri. I acknowledge the Minister of M āori Affairs, Pita Sharples, for putting us 
13772 Motions 26 Sep 2013 
on the map, alongside many others, I am sure, with the Waka M āori, which has 
showcased the many tourism aspects and busin ess links to the USA and indeed to the 
world. It is said that over  300,000 people a day went across th e Oakland Bridge just to 
that location. So there will be benefits desp ite the sadness of the day, I am sure. Hei 
whakakōpani i taku kōrero, me kī, kua kite nei tātou i tēnei tau kua hipa ake, e māia ana 
a Aotearoa ki roto i t ēnei āhuatanga. Ko wai ka m ōhio m ēnā ka hoki atu an ō r ā ki te 
pakanga i te pakanga pai. I te rā nei, ā, me tū tika tātou i te mea, ahakoa kāre i eke, ko te 
ngākau ka taea te kī, ā, i eke ā-ngākau, i eke ā-wairua. Tēnā koutou, kia ora tātou katoa. 
[To close my address, let us say we have witnessed just how resilient New Zealand 
has been in the year just past in regards to this situation. Who is to know whether we 
will ever go back again to engage in the good fight . In respect to this day, we must be 
upright because even though we did not make it, we can still say within us that we made 
it heart and spirit-wise. Congratulations to you collectively, and to us all.] 
Hon JOHN BANKS (Leader—ACT) : On behalf of the ACT Party and the people 
of the Epsom electorate I want to congrat ulate Emirates Team New Zealand on their 
competitive performance in the America’s Cup. I was privileged to be Minister of Sport, 
Fitness and Leisure when the cup arrived from San Diego, and later I handed it over as 
part of a delegation while I was Mayor of Auckland.  
Team New Zealand did not get the result we  wanted, but they s hould be very proud 
of the way they fought right to the end. Dean  Barker, Grant Dalton, and the rest of the 
team worked hard to first win the Loui s Vuitton Cup and then push Oracle Team USA 
right to the end, in a competition that many commentators thought would be all one-way 
traffic. Their graciousness in defeat show s what great sportsmen and ambassadors New 
Zealanders are. Ultimate congratulations  must also go to Oracle Team USA on its 
stunning win of the 34th America’s Cup. Its win will be remembered as one of the great 
sporting comebacks, and it contributed to one of the most exciting America’s Cup races 
in history.  
It is important today that we record and place on the record the huge contribution and 
loyalty of the corporate sponsors. New Z ealand is a nation of sailors, and we can 
appreciate a great competition, which the Am erica’s Cup has proved to be. We did not 
win. However, the innovation and skills of Ne w Zealanders contributed significantly to 
both teams, and that is something we can all be very proud of. 
Hon PETER DUNNE (Leader—United Future) : I rise on behalf of United Future 
to associate myself with the sentiments that  others have expressed during this debate. I 
happen to be one of those curmudgeonly yachting enthusiasts who did not think that the 
advent of these giant catamarans was appropr iate for the America’s Cup tradition, and 
who wondered whether the public would actuall y be seized by the event or would just 
see it as big boys with big toys. The activ ities of Team New Z ealand over the last 
several weeks, and particularly over the last  19 days, have proven to me how wrong my 
fears were. This event has cap tured the public imagination. It was interesting, staring 
out my window in a forlorn moment during the race this morning, to see virtually no 
traffic in the streets of Wellington. People were actually glued to  television sets or 
radios or streaming video, etc., because the nation had taken this event to its heart.  
We wondered a lot over the last week, I guess, how it could be  that on Saturday 
morning we were poised for victory but fo r some fickle wind and running out of time 
when we were just a few seconds away fr om crossing the line, to the situation on 
Thursday, when Team New Zealand, with everyone’s hopes on its back, was fighting 
for grim survival. That is the magic of match racing of this particular calibre. Every tack 
and turn, every twist,  every gybe, every foil, every sail  change, and every tacticians’ 
discussion that we have all been witness to over the last few days has, I think, brought 
home the sheer rush of adrenalin that everyone gets watching this degree of sport.  
26 Sep 2013 Motions 13773 
It is true that this has been described in some quarters as being more a victory for 
technology than for sport. Ce rtainly, technological advancement and the vast amount of 
dollars invested by both teams to bring the latest degree of  technology and skill to their 
operation was relevant, but at the end of the day you cannot take the event away from 
the individual sailors who competed, both for Emirates Team New Zealand and for 
Oracle Team USA. It was their skill, their determination, their raw strength, and their 
courage that achieved the results that they did.  
We can take solace in the performance of  our team, the dignity with which they 
embraced their defeat, and the goodwill that they have created between New Zealand 
and San Francisco. I notice that the Mayor of  San Francisco said today that two great 
things about this cup were, one, that the United States won, and, two, that firm bonds 
were formed with New Zealand by the city of San Francisco. Although we can take all 
of those as positives, we must congratul ate Oracle Team USA on a simply stunning 
performance. And we can note with some satis faction that of the crew members of that 
boat there were, I think, some eight New Zealanders, the boat was built in New Zealand, 
and there is a long New Zealand tradition, so if we want to stretch it, we can claim that 
we all won today. I think there were two Americans on the boat, I say to my colleague.  
What is important now, though, is that we do not wallow in self-pity and gloom 
because of defeat in this contest. We ta ke from it the positives. We congratulate our 
team—Grant Dalton, Dean Barker, and all of them—on a job well done, and we move 
forward. If anyone says that the money that was invested by the Government to achieve 
this result was not money well spent, I comple tely defy that criticism because this has 
been a very positive outcome for New Zealand. The challenge now is to make sure that 
we learn the lessons, that we  regroup, that we get a bette r team together—even better 
next time—and that next time, when we are on match point, we nail the event.  
Motion agreed to. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Acting Leader of the House) : Next week the House is in 
the first week of a 2-week adjournment.  When the House resumes on Tuesday, 15 
October it is the Government’s intention to  progress the Marine Legislation Bill, the 
Copyright (Parallel Importi ng of Films) Amendment Bi ll, the Local Government 
(Auckland Council) Amendment Bill (No 2), and the Telecommunications (Interception 
Capability and Security) Bill.  
GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central): Can I just ask the Acting 
Leader of the House whether there is any intention from the Government to take 
urgency in the next session, particularly for the telecommunications bill? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Acting Leader of the House): No.  
MOTIONS 
Tuvalu Language Week—Recognition 
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): I seek leave to move a motion without 
notice to congratulate the Tuvaluan community of New Zealand— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Leave is sought for that pa rticular course of action. Is there 
any objection? There is none. 
Su’a WILLIAM SIO : I move, That this House congr atulate the Tuvaluan 
community of New Zealand on the inaugural Te Vaiaso o te Gana Tuvalu, Tuvalu 
Language Week, from 30 September to 6 October 2013. The theme is “Tuvalu tau gana 
ko tou lagaifakalaga; Tuvalu, your language keeps your culture and identity afloat”. 
This theme is also a call for New Zealand and the rest of the world to take note that 
13774 Motions 26 Sep 2013 
Tuvalu’s very existence is at stake as the country is in danger of disappearing beneath 
the waves, and the Tuvaluans living in New Z ealand during this week urge the rest of 
the world to do more to combat global wa rming before it sinks their beloved island 
home. 
Motion agreed to. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Hawke’s Bay Water Management—Groundwater Modelling 
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister of Science and 
Innovation: Did GNS Science undertake work modelling the groundwater in the 
Ruataniwha Plains in 2012 and 2013; and was the contract completed fully? 
Hon NIKKI KAYE (Minister for Food Safety)  on behalf of the Minister of 
Science and Innovation : Yes, I have been advised that GNS Science undertook 
groundwater modelling work in relation to the Ruataniwha Plains during the 2012-13 
year. I am advised GNS Science was contra cted by the Hawke’s Bay Regional Council 
for four separate pieces of work. Three contracts were completed and invoiced. One 
piece of work was not completed. 
Dr Russel Norman : Did the Minister know that GNS  Science scientists raised 
serious concerns about the accuracy of the regional council’s groundwater model, the 
fundamental information underpinning the work? 
Hon NIKKI KAYE: I am advised that the Hawke’ s Bay Regional Council opted to 
change its management strategy for the Ruatan iwha Plains. That is the reason that has 
been given. 
Dr Russel Norman: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I invite the member to repeat his question. 
Dr Russel Norman : Did the Minister know that GNS  Science scientists raised 
serious concerns about the accuracy of the regional council’s groundwater model, which 
was the fundamental information underpinning the report? 
Hon NIKKI KAYE : Just to build on my previous answer, I have said the reason 
why the contract was terminated, but fr om my perspective—and I am obviously 
answering on behalf of the Minister—he did not know that. 
Dr Russel Norman : Were the GNS Science scientists working on the project 
pressured by the regional council into completing a report on the dam, despite their 
objecting strenuously to the accuracy of the information they were supplied to work 
with by the regional council? 
Hon NIKKI KAYE : The first thing that I would say is that the contractual 
arrangements—and I want to make this poi nt—between GNS Science and the Hawke’s 
Bay Regional Council are not something that Ministers would ever be involved in the 
detail of, but the member does make an alle gation in his particular question. I have no 
knowledge of that allegation. 
Dr Russel Norman : Did GNS Science scientists insi st on recording their concerns 
about the inaccuracy of the council’s groundwater model in  their updated report, at 
which point the contract was terminated by the council? 
Hon NIKKI KAYE : I will just repeat what I have said before, which is that GNS 
Science has hundreds of contracts. The first time I became aware of this issue was 
today, so what the member is saying in te rms of his question I cannot verify. But I

INSOLVENCY PRACTITIONERS BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon CRAIG FOSS (Minister of Commerce) : I move, That the Insolvency 
Practitioners Bill be  now read a second time . Insolvency practitioners carry out a 
number of different insolvency proce sses, including liqui dations, voluntary 
administrations, and receiverships. These pr ocesses require a practitioner to carry out 
skilled tasks with sound judgment and integr ity in order to protect and promote an 
efficient and effective corporate insolvency system. There is general consensus amongst 
reputable insolvency practitioners that there is a small number of practitioners who are 
continually underperforming and imposing si gnificant costs upon cr editors and failing 
to discharge their statutory obligations. These problems revolve around competency, 
unethical behaviour, and insufficient monitoring.  
The Insolvency Practitioners Bill wa s drafted in 2008 under the previous 
Government to create a negative licensing regi me to regulate insolvency practitioners. 
Negative licensing would enable  any person to prac tise as an insolvency practitioner 
unless they were prohibited. It was seen as a low-cost, light-handed regulatory approach 
to strengthen an enforcement void: the abil ity to remove incompetent and dishonest 
insolvency practitioners from the market.  
The Commerce Committee considered the bill at  the end of 2010 and in the first part 
of 2011. I would like to thank the committee for the constructive time spent undertaking 
a thorough examination of the bill. The bill received 11 submissions and most 
submitters did not think the bill went far enough to address the problems in the 
insolvency market. Submitters argued that in  the intervening time, the global financial 
crisis had meant that there was an increase in insolvency work and an increase in the 
number of insolvency practitioners taking a ppointments. This meant that the magnitude 
of the problems had become more evident. The select committee carefully considered 
options for regulating insolvency practitioners and reported back to the House on 9 May 
2011 its recommendation to adopt a registratio n model, instead of a negative licensing 
regime.  
Under the bill as reported back, all insolv ency practitioners will now be required to 
be registered in order to accept insolvency appointments. The Registrar of Companies 
will have enhanced oversight and enforcem ent mechanisms, including the power to 
deregister substandard or delinquent individuals. I suppor t this recommendation. It is 
important that corporate insolvencies are car ried out professionally and efficiently. This 
bill is part of the Government’s focus on improving the integrity of our financial 
systems. It is important that we boost inve stor confidence and that investors have the 
confidence in our markets. It is especially important that investors know that if an 
insolvency practitioner is goi ng to look into the affairs of a company, they can have 
confidence that it can be done and will be done with integr ity, and that the insolvency 
practitioner has the minimum skills for the job.  
A register held by the company’s office will give the public access to basic and 
standardised information about practitioners  who are registered. Through the register, 
the Registrar of Companies will be able to collect information and regulate practitioners 
more effectively. The bill is set to come into force 9 months after the date on which it 
26 Sep 2013 Insolvency Practitioners Bill 13821 
receives the Royal assent. Insolvency practitioners have up to 3 months after this to 
register. The operation of the registration regi me will be reviewed no later than 4 years 
after the legislation comes into force to r ecommend whether any further amendments to 
the regime would be necessary or desirable. More specifically, the bill as reported back 
will amend the Companies Act 1993 and the Receiverships Act 1993 to make clear how 
the appointment of insolvency practitione rs to, and the removal of insolvency 
practitioners from, the register will work. There will be new provisions, including the 
eligibility criteria, enhanced duties, and criteria for disqualification, and an appropriate 
range of penalties for failure to comply with statutory obligations. Under the 
amendments, a person can apply for a court order to override any removal from the 
register. 
 One important amendment is greater transparency so that creditors must be provided 
with relevant information by insolvency prac titioners at the earliest opportunity. This 
includes a statement of interest by the insolvency practitioner and an additional report to 
the registrar that summarises the insolvency. This new regime will be a significant 
improvement and will help with the rec ognition and detection of incompetent and 
unethical persons, who will either be prevented from registering or have their 
registration cancelled.  
A substantial amount of work has been goi ng on behind the scenes since the bill was 
reported back from the select committee. I am pleased that this bill is now continuing its 
progression through the House. At th e appropriate time I will introduce a 
Supplementary Order Paper that proposes further amendments to the bill to better align 
requirements for the different types of pract itioners and clarify the obligations of 
practitioners. I commend this bill to the House.
